On this page

    Start here: six through-lines, five eras and how to read the evidence

    In this chapter

    • Name the six quantities that every generation of recommendation and ads algorithms changed: signal, model, objective, serving architecture, pricing and measurement.
    • Place any method from 1992 to 2026 in one of five eras and say which bottleneck it removed.
    • Grade a claim by its evidence: peer-reviewed result, company engineering post, earnings-call statement or this reader's inference.
    • Pick the gist path or the full path.

    The gist. Recommendation and advertising are one problem seen from two sides: choose, for one person at one moment, a few items out of millions, using feedback that the previous choices produced. Every generation of algorithms was forced by a bottleneck in the one before it: too little signal, too little model capacity, the wrong objective, too slow a serving path, a pricing rule that rewarded the wrong behaviour, or a measurement that could not tell correlation from cause. Read each era as an answer to the previous era's bottleneck, and each claim with its evidence grade attached.

    One problem, two business models

    A recommender and an ad system solve the same allocation problem; they differ in who supplies the items and who pays for the slot. A recommender ranks items the platform owns or hosts (videos, products, posts) to maximize some long-run user value. An ad system ranks items that third parties pay to insert, so the ranking score multiplies a predicted response by a price the advertiser sets or the platform derives, and the platform must also run an auction, charge a price, pace a budget and prove that the ads caused sales. Since about 2016 the two have converged: the same deep ranking models, the same retrieval stack and, in 2024–2025, the same generative architectures serve both organic and paid slots at Meta, Google, ByteDance, Kuaishou and Alibaba.

    Throughout, an impression is one display of one item to one user; CTR (click-through rate) is clicks per impression; CVR (conversion rate) is conversions per click unless stated otherwise; eCPM is expected revenue per 1,000 impressions. The companion Computational Advertising reader covers contracts, cash flow and auctions in depth; this reader follows how the algorithms changed over time.

    Six through-lines

    Six quantities changed in every era; tracking them is the fastest way to understand why a method appeared when it did.

    Through-line1990s2006–20132014–20202021–2026
    SignalExplicit ratings from a few thousand usersRatings at scale (Netflix: 100M); implicit clicks and purchases; sparse categorical ad logsBehaviour sequences, dense embeddings, multimodal contentLifelong action streams of thousands to tens of thousands of events; privacy-limited cross-app signal
    ModelNeighbourhoods (user–user, item–item)Matrix factorization; logistic regression on billions of hashed features; factorization machinesEmbedding + MLP + explicit feature crosses; attention over behaviour; two-tower retrievalTransformer-style sequence models, generative retrieval over semantic IDs, foundation models distilled into serving models
    ObjectivePredict a ratingRMSE (Netflix), pairwise ranking (BPR), calibrated CTR (log loss)Multi-task: click, watch time, conversion, satisfactionNext-action generation; long-term value; advertiser value under constraints
    ServingOne scored listPrecomputed item–item tables; online linear scoringMulti-stage cascade: retrieval → pre-rank → rank → re-rank, with approximate nearest-neighbour searchFewer, larger stages; some end-to-end generative pipelines
    Pricing (ads)CPM banners; GoTo.com pay-per-click, pay-your-bidQuality-weighted second-price auctions (GSP); real-time bidding exchangesOptimized CPM/CPC (oCPM, oCPC); move to first-price in displayAutobidding to target CPA/ROAS; campaign automation (Performance Max, Advantage+)
    MeasurementOffline accuracy on held-out ratingsOnline A/B tests; replay evaluation for banditsDebiasing (position, selection), off-policy correction; reproducibility auditsPrivacy-constrained attribution (ATT, SKAdNetwork); scaling-law curves; incrementality

    Pitfall: hindsight ordering

    The table reads like a clean sequence, but generations overlapped for years. Logistic regression ran production ad ranking at Google well after deep models were published, item–item tables still power “customers also bought” lists, and gradient-boosted trees still win many tabular tasks. A new method usually displaced the old one first in the stage where its bottleneck hurt most.

    Five eras, each answering the last one's bottleneck

    The eras are defined by the bottleneck their methods removed, not by calendar years; the dates are when the defining work appeared.

    1. 1992–2005
      Neighbourhoods and keyword auctions. Bottleneck removed: no way to personalize at all. Collaborative filtering uses other people's ratings; GoTo.com and Google AdWords sell clicks on keywords by auction.
    2. 2006–2013
      Factorization and planet-scale linear models. Bottleneck removed: sparsity. Latent factors generalize across users and items that never co-occurred; hashed logistic regression trained online handles billions of ad features.
    3. 2013–2020
      Deep learning and the multi-stage funnel. Bottleneck removed: hand-built feature crosses and a single scoring stage. Embeddings, learned interactions and two-tower retrieval scale to billions of items.
    4. 2009–2025
      Exchanges, first-price auctions and autobidding (ads track) and bias, causality and privacy (cross-cutting). Bottlenecks removed: advertisers bidding by hand, and models trained on their own biased logs; then a new constraint imposed from outside: loss of cross-app identifiers.
    5. 2021–2026
      Scaling and generative recommenders. Bottleneck removed: ranking models whose quality stopped improving with more compute. Sequence transducers and generative retrieval show compute-scaling curves similar to language models.

    The interactive timeline lists every dated milestone in one place, filterable by track and era.

    Every claim carries an evidence grade

    Industrial recommender research mixes peer-reviewed results with marketing; this reader labels which is which. The four grades:

    GradeWhat it meansHow much to trust it
    PaperPeer-reviewed or widely cited paper with the method describedThe method is as described. Reported online gains are the authors' A/B tests on their own baselines and cannot be reproduced outside the company.
    PostCompany engineering blog, product documentation, press release or contemporaneous news recordDates and architecture outlines are usually accurate; performance numbers are selected and baselines unspecified.
    CallEarnings call, investor letter or press statementDirectionally informative about what management attributes revenue to; not evidence of mechanism.
    InferenceThis reader's interpretationArgued from the sources but not stated in them; flagged explicitly.

    A recurring lesson from chapter 5: several celebrated neural gains shrank or vanished once baselines were tuned properly. Treat an unreproduced online uplift as a hypothesis.

    The timeline: every dated milestone, 1992–2026

    In this chapter

    • Filter the milestones by track (recommendation, ads, systems, evaluation and bias, privacy) and by era, or search by keyword.
    • For each milestone read what changed, why it mattered and its evidence grade, then follow the link to the chapter that explains it.
    • Notice the lags: a method's paper, its production adoption and its displacement are often years apart.

    The gist. Read the timeline once from top to bottom with all tracks on: the recommendation and ads tracks run in parallel until about 2016 and then merge into one modelling stack, while the privacy track arrives from outside and reshapes the ads track after 2017. Then filter to a single track to see its internal logic: each entry answers a limitation of an earlier one.

    Patterns worth noticing

    • Industry first, theory second, in auctions. GSP ran from 2002; its equilibrium analysis appeared in 2007. The same happened with autobidding (products from 2007, theory from 2019).
    • Theory first, industry later, in evaluation. Propensity weighting and off-policy estimators existed for years before they appeared in production recommenders around 2017–2019.
    • Convergence around 2016. Before it, recommendation papers optimized RMSE and ranking metrics while ads papers optimized calibrated CTR; after it, the same architectures (Wide & Deep, DCN, DIN, MMoE) are used for both.
    • Exogenous shocks. The privacy entries are the only ones not driven by an algorithmic bottleneck, and they changed the ads track more than any single model did.

    Era I (1992–2005): neighbourhoods and keyword auctions

    In this chapter

    • Write the GroupLens user–user prediction and say why it does not scale.
    • Explain the complexity argument that made item–item filtering Amazon's production choice.
    • Explain why GoTo.com's pay-your-bid auction produced bidding cycles, and how Google's 2002 quality-weighted second-price rule changed both the ranking and the incentives.
    • Compute GSP and VCG payments for a two-slot auction and state the Edelman–Ostrovsky–Schwarz equivalence.

    The gist. The first recommenders replaced editors with neighbours: people who rated things like you did predict what you will like. That worked for a few thousand Usenet readers but not for tens of millions of shoppers, so Amazon flipped the neighbourhood from users to items and precomputed it offline. Advertising went through the same shift from manual to computed. GoTo.com auctioned search positions to the highest bidder, which produced unstable bidding wars and showed ads nobody clicked. Google ranked by bid times predicted click rate and charged each winner the minimum needed to keep its position. That one rule made click prediction the core of search advertising.

    Collaborative filtering: other people's ratings as the signal

    Collaborative filtering predicts a user's interest from the recorded interest of similar users, with no model of the item's content. Xerox PARC's Tapestry (Goldberg, Nichols, Oki and Terry, 1992) coined the term: users annotated e-mail and Usenet messages, and others filtered by those annotations with explicit queries such as “messages Joe liked”. Filtering was collaborative but manual: you had to know whose judgement to trust.

    GroupLens (Resnick et al., 1994) automated the choice of whom to trust. Each Usenet reader rated articles 1–5; a server predicted unseen ratings as the user's mean plus a correlation-weighted average of other users' deviations from their own means:

    r^u,i=rˉu+∑v∈N(u)wuv (rv,i−rˉv)∑v∈N(u)∣wuv∣,wuv=corr⁡(ru,⋅, rv,⋅) over co-rated items.\hat r_{u,i}=\bar r_u+\frac{\sum_{v\in N(u)} w_{uv}\,(r_{v,i}-\bar r_v)}{\sum_{v\in N(u)} |w_{uv}|},\qquad w_{uv}=\operatorname{corr}(r_{u,\cdot},\,r_{v,\cdot})\text{ over co-rated items}.r^u,i​=rˉu​+∑v∈N(u)​∣wuv​∣∑v∈N(u)​wuv​(rv,i​−rˉv​)​,wuv​=corr(ru,⋅​,rv,⋅​) over co-rated items.

    Here rv,ir_{v,i}rv,i​ is user vvv's rating of item iii, rˉv\bar r_vrˉv​ that user's mean rating and N(u)N(u)N(u) the neighbours who rated iii. Mean-centring removes the fact that some people rate everything a 4. MIT's Ringo (Shardanand and Maes, 1995) applied the same idea to music and compared similarity measures, an early example of the field's habit of tuning the similarity function.

    The user–user method has two structural problems. First, cost: predicting for one user scans all other users, and with MMM users and NNN items the naive cost per prediction is O(MN)O(MN)O(MN). Second, sparsity: two shoppers in a catalogue of millions rarely share enough purchases for a correlation to mean anything, so neighbourhoods are noisy exactly where most users are.

    Item–item filtering: move the neighbourhood offline

    Amazon's item-to-item filtering made recommendation cheap at serving time by precomputing a similar-items table offline. Sarwar, Karypis, Konstan and Riedl (WWW 2001) evaluated item-based neighbourhoods academically; Linden, Smith and York (IEEE Internet Computing, 2003) described the production system at Amazon. Represent each item by its vector of customers (1 if bought). Similarity is the cosine between item vectors:

    sim⁡(X,Y)=x⋅y∥x∥ ∥y∥.\operatorname{sim}(X,Y)=\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y}{\lVert\mathbf x\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf y\rVert}.sim(X,Y)=∥x∥∥y∥x⋅y​.
    Worked example

    Three items, four customers

    Given: purchase vectors over customers 1–4: x=(1,1,0,1)\mathbf x=(1,1,0,1)x=(1,1,0,1), y=(1,1,0,0)\mathbf y=(1,1,0,0)y=(1,1,0,0), z=(0,0,1,1)\mathbf z=(0,0,1,1)z=(0,0,1,1).

    1. sim⁡(X,Y)=23 2=22.449=0.816.\operatorname{sim}(X,Y)=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3\,\sqrt2}=\dfrac{2}{2.449}=0.816.sim(X,Y)=3​2​2​=2.4492​=0.816.
    2. sim⁡(X,Z)=13 2=0.408.\operatorname{sim}(X,Z)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3\,\sqrt2}=0.408.sim(X,Z)=3​2​1​=0.408.
    3. sim⁡(Y,Z)=0\operatorname{sim}(Y,Z)=0sim(Y,Z)=0: no shared customers.

    Result: a customer who just bought Y is shown X first, then nothing from Z. The table row for Y is [X:0.816, Z:0][X:0.816,\ Z:0][X:0.816, Z:0], computed once offline.

    Check: cosine is 1 only for identical vectors; X and Y differ only in customer 4, so a high but not perfect score is right.

    The complexity argument is what made the choice. Linden et al. note that building the table is O(N2M)O(N^2M)O(N2M) in the worst case but close to O(NM)O(NM)O(NM) in practice, because most customers buy few items. At serving time, the cost depends only on how many items this user has bought, not on the size of the catalogue or the customer base. Item similarities also change slowly (a book's co-purchasers are stable), so the table can be refreshed in batch, whereas a user's neighbourhood shifts with every purchase.

    What survived

    Precompute what is stable, compute at request time only what depends on the request: this split became the retrieval/ranking split of chapter 5. YouTube's 2010 system (Davidson et al., RecSys 2010) was still item–item at heart, using co-visitation counts within a session normalized by item popularity, then ranking the candidates.

    Content-based filtering was the alternative, and its weakness is the mirror image of collaborative filtering's. Representing items by their attributes (keywords with TF-IDF weights, genre tags, Pandora's hand-labelled Music Genome Project from 2000) handles new items with no interactions, the cold-start problem. But it recommends more of what you already consumed and cannot discover that people who like jazz also tend to buy a certain cookbook. Hybrids that combine both are the norm from this point on.

    Advertising before auctions: the CPM banner

    The first web ads were sold like magazine space, priced per thousand impressions and targeted by site section. HotWired ran the first widely cited clickable banner in October 1994 (for AT&T). Ad servers such as DoubleClick (founded 1996) delivered and counted impressions; targeting was by site, section and coarse user attributes, and the price was negotiated. There was no per-impression prediction because the advertiser, not the platform, bore the risk that nobody clicked.

    GoTo.com: pay-per-click, pay-your-bid, and the bidding cycle

    GoTo.com (1998) sold search-result positions by auction, charging per click and ranking purely by bid, and the auction had no stable equilibrium. Advertisers bid on keywords; the highest bidder took position 1 and paid its own bid per click (a generalized first-price auction). Two problems followed.

    • Bidding cycles. With bids changeable at any time, each bidder wants to bid one cent above the next bidder below it, not its full value. Two rivals ratchet each other upward until one reaches its value; that one drops to the minimum bid; the leader then drops to one cent above it, and the climb restarts. Edelman and Ostrovsky (2007) documented these sawtooth patterns in Overture's bid logs. Revenue and allocation both suffered from the churn.
    • Ranking ignores clicks. Under pay-per-click the platform earns only when users click. Ranking a $2 ad with a 1% click rate above a $1 ad with a 3% click rate loses money for the platform and shows users a less relevant ad.

    GoTo became Overture in 2001 and was bought by Yahoo in 2003; Overture had moved to second-price (GSP) billing in mid-2002 (sources).

    Google's 2002 rule: rank by bid × CTR, pay the next bidder's price

    Google's AdWords Select (2002) ranked ads by expected revenue per impression and charged each winner the smallest bid that would keep its position; the price became a function of predicted click rates. Let advertiser kkk bid bkb_kbk​ per click and have predicted click rate ckc_kck​. Sort by bkckb_k c_kbk​ck​ (the eCPM divided by 1,000). The ad in position iii pays, per click,

    pi=bi+1 ci+1ci,p_i=\frac{b_{i+1}\,c_{i+1}}{c_i},pi​=ci​bi+1​ci+1​​,

    the bid at which its score would tie the next ad's. This is the generalized second-price (GSP) auction with quality weighting. From August 2005 Google folded more than click rate into a Quality Score that also set each keyword's minimum bid.

    Worked example

    One slot, quality-weighted

    Given: ad A bids $2.00 per click with cA=0.01c_A=0.01cA​=0.01; ad B bids $1.00 with cB=0.03c_B=0.03cB​=0.03.

    1. Scores: bAcA=$0.020b_Ac_A=\$0.020bA​cA​=$0.020, bBcB=$0.030b_Bc_B=\$0.030bB​cB​=$0.030 per impression. B wins despite the lower bid.
    2. B's price per click: pB=2.00×0.010.03=$0.667.p_B=\dfrac{2.00\times0.01}{0.03}=\$0.667.pB​=0.032.00×0.01​=$0.667.
    3. Expected revenue per impression: cB pB=0.03×$0.667=$0.020.c_B\,p_B=0.03\times\$0.667=\$0.020.cB​pB​=0.03×$0.667=$0.020.

    Result: B pays $0.67 per click, and the platform's expected revenue per impression equals A's score, $0.020.

    Check: in expectation the winner pays the runner-up's expected revenue per impression, exactly the second-price logic applied in score space. Ranking by bid alone would have shown A for an expected $0.020 per impression and a third of the clicks.

    Why this made CTR prediction the core business

    The predicted click rate ckc_kck​ now enters both the ranking and the price. An over-estimate for one ad promotes it and also lowers the price it pays (cic_ici​ is in the denominator). Every later generation of CTR models in chapter 4 and chapter 5 is judged first by calibration, not only ranking accuracy, for this reason.

    GSP is not truthful, yet often lands on the VCG outcome

    Bidding your true value is not an equilibrium strategy in GSP, but a natural class of GSP equilibria yields exactly the VCG payments. In a position auction, slot jjj gets αj\alpha_jαj​ clicks per impression (position effect), the same for every ad (set quality equal to keep the example clean). The Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (VCG) mechanism charges each winner the value the others lose because of its presence; truthful bidding is dominant.

    Worked example

    Two slots, three bidders

    Given: slot click rates α1=0.10\alpha_1=0.10α1​=0.10, α2=0.05\alpha_2=0.05α2​=0.05; values per click v=($10,$6,$2)v=(\$10,\$6,\$2)v=($10,$6,$2).

    1. GSP with truthful bids: slot 1 pays $6 per click, slot 2 pays $2. Revenue per impression 0.10×6+0.05×2=$0.70.0.10\times6+0.05\times2=\$0.70.0.10×6+0.05×2=$0.70.
    2. VCG, bidder 2: without it, bidder 3 would take slot 2 and earn 0.05×2=$0.100.05\times2=\$0.100.05×2=$0.10; bidder 2's charge is $0.10 per impression, i.e. $2 per click.
    3. VCG, bidder 1: without it, bidders 2 and 3 get 0.10×6+0.05×2=$0.700.10\times6+0.05\times2=\$0.700.10×6+0.05×2=$0.70; with it they get 0.05×6=$0.300.05\times6=\$0.300.05×6=$0.30. Charge $0.40 per impression, i.e. $4 per click.
    4. VCG revenue: $0.40+$0.10=$0.50\$0.40+\$0.10=\$0.50$0.40+$0.10=$0.50 per impression.
    5. Is truthful GSP an equilibrium? Bidder 1 pays $6 in slot 1, utility 0.10×(10−6)=$0.400.10\times(10-6)=\$0.400.10×(10−6)=$0.40. By bidding between $2 and $6 it drops to slot 2, pays $2, utility 0.05×(10−2)=$0.400.05\times(10-2)=\$0.400.05×(10−2)=$0.40: indifferent here, and with slightly different numbers strictly better. Truth-telling is not dominant.
    6. Equilibrium with VCG prices: bidder 2 bids $4 instead of $6, bidder 3 bids $2. Bidder 1 pays $4 (utility $0.60, versus $0.40 in slot 2), bidder 2 pays $2 (utility $0.20) and does not envy bidder 1's slot at bidder 1's price, since 0.10×(6−4)=$0.200.10\times(6-4)=\$0.200.10×(6−4)=$0.20 as well. Bidder 3 could take slot 2 only by bidding above $4, and would then pay $4 per click, above its $2 value. No one gains by deviating.

    Result: truthful GSP would raise $0.70 per impression; VCG raises $0.50; the equilibrium in step 6 is a GSP outcome with exactly the VCG payments.

    Check: the VCG price of slot 1 ($4 per click) is the price at which bidder 2 is indifferent between slot 1 at $4 and slot 2 at $2: 0.10(6−4)=0.05(6−2)=0.200.10(6-4)=0.05(6-2)=0.200.10(6−4)=0.05(6−2)=0.20.

    Edelman, Ostrovsky and Schwarz (2007) and Varian (2007) formalized this independently: GSP has a family of “locally envy-free” (Varian: symmetric Nash) equilibria, and the one with the lowest revenue gives each advertiser the same position and payment as VCG. This is a named result, not proved here. In practice GSP survived in search for two decades because it was simple to explain (“pay just enough to beat the next ad”) and, at equilibrium, no worse for revenue than VCG. Google moved its contextual (AdSense) ads to a version of VCG in late 2012 while search stayed on GSP, and Facebook's ad auction is a VCG auction (Varian and Harris, 2014).

    What broke next

    Both halves of Era I hit the same wall: they needed a dense signal that did not exist. Neighbourhood methods need overlapping histories; most users and items have almost none. Quality-weighted auctions need a predicted click rate for every ad, query and user, including ads with no history. Both pushed the field toward models that generalize across sparse observations: latent factors for ratings and large-scale regression for clicks, the subject of Era II.

    Era II (2006–2013): latent factors and planet-scale linear models

    In this chapter

    • Say what the Netflix Prize did and did not change, and write the biased matrix-factorization objective with its SGD update.
    • Derive the implicit-feedback ALS trick that makes summing over all unobserved cells affordable.
    • State BPR's pairwise objective and its relation to AUC.
    • Derive the factorization-machine identity that cuts pairwise interactions from O(kn2)O(kn^2)O(kn2) to O(kn)O(kn)O(kn).
    • Explain why ad click prediction ran on online logistic regression (AdPredictor, FTRL-Proximal, hashing, GBDT features) and why contextual bandits appeared.

    The gist. Two separate communities attacked sparsity. Recommender researchers, galvanized by Netflix's $1M prize, learned a short latent vector per user and per item so that two users who never rated the same film could still be compared. Ad engineers, facing billions of sparse features and models retrained every few minutes, chose the simplest model that could keep up: logistic regression, trained online with per-coordinate learning rates and L1 sparsity, often fed by hashed or tree-derived features. Factorization machines joined the two lines by giving every feature a latent vector. Bandits addressed the remaining gap: a model trained on its own past choices never learns about the options it never shows.

    The Netflix Prize turned recommendation into a leaderboard

    From October 2006 to September 2009 Netflix offered $1 million to whoever cut the RMSE of its Cinematch rating predictor by 10% on a hidden test set; the competition popularized latent-factor models and ensembling, and showed the limits of RMSE as a business objective. The data were about 100 million ratings (1–5 stars) from about 480,000 users on 17,770 films. Cinematch scored a test RMSE of about 0.9525; the target was 0.8572. Annual progress prizes went to the BellKor team (8.43% in 2007) and to the merged team BellKor in BigChaos (9.44% in 2008), both measured against Cinematch on the public quiz set (RMSE 0.9514). The grand prize went to BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos with a test RMSE of 0.8567, a 10.06% improvement, tying the runner-up's score but submitted earlier (sources).

    Netflix adopted two of the component models, not the winning ensemble. Its 2012 engineering post explains that matrix factorization and restricted Boltzmann machines went into production after the first progress prize, but the extra accuracy of the full blend did not justify the engineering cost; by then the product had shifted from mailed DVDs and star ratings to streaming, where what people play matters more than how they rate. The lesson that the competition's offline metric was not the business metric recurs in every later era. A second contest was cancelled in 2010 after researchers showed that the “anonymized” ratings could be linked to public IMDb reviews (Narayanan and Shmatikov, 2008), an early warning for chapter 7.

    Matrix factorization: a short vector per user and per item

    Matrix factorization models each rating as a global mean plus user and item biases plus a dot product of learned kkk-dimensional factors, fitted only on observed ratings. Simon Funk's December 2006 blog post showed that plain stochastic gradient descent on the observed entries, with no imputation, moved quickly up the leaderboard; Koren, Bell and Volinsky (IEEE Computer, 2009) is the standard account. With K\mathcal KK the set of observed (user, item) pairs:

    min⁡b,p,q∑(u,i)∈K(rui−μ−bu−bi−pu⊤qi)2+λ(bu2+bi2+∥pu∥2+∥qi∥2).\min_{b,p,q}\sum_{(u,i)\in\mathcal K}\bigl(r_{ui}-\mu-b_u-b_i-\mathbf p_u^{\top}\mathbf q_i\bigr)^2+\lambda\bigl(b_u^2+b_i^2+\lVert\mathbf p_u\rVert^2+\lVert\mathbf q_i\rVert^2\bigr).b,p,qmin​(u,i)∈K∑​(rui​−μ−bu​−bi​−pu⊤​qi​)2+λ(bu2​+bi2​+∥pu​∥2+∥qi​∥2).

    For one observed rating with error eui=rui−r^uie_{ui}=r_{ui}-\hat r_{ui}eui​=rui​−r^ui​ and step size γ\gammaγ, the SGD update is

    bu←bu+γ(eui−λbu),pu←pu+γ(eui qi−λpu),bi←bi+γ(eui−λbi),qi←qi+γ(eui pu−λqi).\begin{aligned}b_u&\leftarrow b_u+\gamma(e_{ui}-\lambda b_u), & \mathbf p_u&\leftarrow\mathbf p_u+\gamma(e_{ui}\,\mathbf q_i-\lambda\mathbf p_u),\\ b_i&\leftarrow b_i+\gamma(e_{ui}-\lambda b_i), & \mathbf q_i&\leftarrow\mathbf q_i+\gamma(e_{ui}\,\mathbf p_u-\lambda\mathbf q_i).\end{aligned}bu​bi​​←bu​+γ(eui​−λbu​),←bi​+γ(eui​−λbi​),​pu​qi​​←pu​+γ(eui​qi​−λpu​),←qi​+γ(eui​pu​−λqi​).​

    (The constant factor 2 from differentiating the square is absorbed into γ\gammaγ.) Why it generalizes where neighbourhoods do not: two users who share no films still get comparable vectors if their films' vectors are similar, because the item vectors are shared across everyone. The Prize then drove a series of refinements by Koren: SVD++ (KDD 2008) adds a term built from which films a user rated, regardless of the rating, an implicit signal; timeSVD++ (KDD 2009) lets biases and factors drift over time.

    Pitfall: “SVD” is a misnomer here

    Netflix-era “SVD” is not the singular value decomposition: SVD is undefined on a matrix with 99% missing entries, and imputing zeros would treat “not rated” as “hated”. The model is a regularized low-rank fit on observed cells only.

    Implicit feedback: every unobserved cell matters, and ALS makes that affordable

    For clicks, plays and purchases there are no negative ratings, so the model must use the unobserved cells; Hu, Koren and Volinsky (ICDM 2008) made this tractable with a weighted least-squares trick. Define a binary preference pui=1p_{ui}=1pui​=1 if user uuu consumed item iii at all, else 0, and a confidence cui=1+αruic_{ui}=1+\alpha r_{ui}cui​=1+αrui​ that grows with the amount consumed ruir_{ui}rui​. The loss sums over all M×NM\times NM×N cells:

    min⁡X,Y∑u,icui (pui−xu⊤yi)2+λ(∑u∥xu∥2+∑i∥yi∥2).\min_{X,Y}\sum_{u,i}c_{ui}\,\bigl(p_{ui}-\mathbf x_u^{\top}\mathbf y_i\bigr)^2+\lambda\Bigl(\sum_u\lVert\mathbf x_u\rVert^2+\sum_i\lVert\mathbf y_i\rVert^2\Bigr).X,Ymin​u,i∑​cui​(pui​−xu⊤​yi​)2+λ(u∑​∥xu​∥2+i∑​∥yi​∥2).

    With item factors YYY (an N×kN\times kN×k matrix) fixed, each user's vector has a closed form, xu=(Y⊤CuY+λI)−1Y⊤Cupu\mathbf x_u=(Y^{\top}C^uY+\lambda I)^{-1}Y^{\top}C^u\mathbf p_uxu​=(Y⊤CuY+λI)−1Y⊤Cupu​, where CuC^uCu is diagonal with entries cuic_{ui}cui​. Computed naively, Y⊤CuYY^{\top}C^uYY⊤CuY costs O(k2N)O(k^2N)O(k2N) per user. The trick:

    Y⊤CuY=Y⊤Y⏟same for all users+  Y⊤(Cu−I) Y,Y^{\top}C^uY=\underbrace{Y^{\top}Y}_{\text{same for all users}}+\;Y^{\top}(C^u-I)\,Y,Y⊤CuY=same for all usersY⊤Y​​+Y⊤(Cu−I)Y,

    and Cu−IC^u-ICu−I is nonzero only on the nun_unu​ items the user consumed. So one O(k2N)O(k^2N)O(k2N) computation of Y⊤YY^{\top}YY⊤Y per sweep is shared, and each user costs O(k2nu+k3)O(k^2n_u+k^3)O(k2nu​+k3). A full sweep over users costs O(k2∣K∣+k3M)O(k^2|\mathcal K|+k^3M)O(k2∣K∣+k3M), linear in the number of observed interactions, even though the loss touches every cell. Alternating with the symmetric item step gives alternating least squares (ALS), which parallelizes trivially and became the standard implicit-feedback baseline (Spark MLlib's ALS implements it).

    BPR: optimize the ranking, not the reconstruction

    Bayesian Personalized Ranking (Rendle et al., UAI 2009) trains on pairs: a consumed item should score above an unconsumed one for the same user. For triples (u,i,j)(u,i,j)(u,i,j) with iii observed and jjj sampled from the unobserved items, and any scoring model x^ui\hat x_{ui}x^ui​:

    max⁡Θ∑(u,i,j)ln⁡σ(x^ui−x^uj)−λ∥Θ∥2,σ(z)=11+e−z.\max_\Theta\sum_{(u,i,j)}\ln\sigma\bigl(\hat x_{ui}-\hat x_{uj}\bigr)-\lambda\lVert\Theta\rVert^2,\qquad \sigma(z)=\frac1{1+e^{-z}}.Θmax​(u,i,j)∑​lnσ(x^ui​−x^uj​)−λ∥Θ∥2,σ(z)=1+e−z1​.

    The per-user AUC is the fraction of (observed, unobserved) pairs ranked correctly, 1∣Pu∣∑1[x^ui>x^uj]\frac1{|P_u|}\sum\mathbb 1[\hat x_{ui}>\hat x_{uj}]∣Pu​∣1​∑1[x^ui​>x^uj​]; BPR replaces the step function with the smooth surrogate ln⁡σ\ln\sigmalnσ. Sampling negatives instead of summing over all of them is the idea that returns, at much larger scale, as in-batch negatives in two-tower retrieval.

    Click prediction for ads: logistic regression that never stops training

    Ad click models of this era were logistic regressions over billions of sparse binary features, trained online, because freshness and calibration mattered more than model class. A feature is typically an indicator for a value or a cross of values (query word × ad id, user country × advertiser). The model is p(click∣x)=σ(w⊤x)p(\text{click}\mid\mathbf x)=\sigma(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x)p(click∣x)=σ(w⊤x), trained on log loss. Landmarks:

    • Microsoft, 2007. Richardson, Dominowska and Ragno (WWW 2007) predicted click rates for new search ads from ad text and term features, the cold-start problem of the quality-weighted auction.
    • Bing's AdPredictor, 2010. Graepel et al. (ICML 2010) used Bayesian probit regression with a Gaussian belief per weight, updated online by approximate message passing in a factor graph; it served all of Bing's sponsored-search traffic from 2009. The posterior variance doubles as an uncertainty estimate, useful for exploration.
    • Feature hashing, 2009. Weinberger et al. (ICML 2009) mapped raw feature strings to a fixed-size weight vector with a hash function, so the model never needs a feature dictionary; collisions behave like a small amount of noise. This became the default way to handle open-ended vocabularies.
    • Google's FTRL-Proximal, 2013. McMahan et al., “Ad click prediction: a view from the trenches” (KDD 2013), is the reference for production practice.
    • Facebook, 2014. He et al. (ADKDD 2014) fed the leaf indices of boosted decision trees into a logistic regression: the trees learn non-linear feature crosses offline, the linear model trains online. The paper also showed that prediction quality decayed measurably as the model went stale, so retraining frequency was a first-order design choice.

    FTRL-Proximal gives per-coordinate learning rates with exact zeros, so the model stays sparse enough to serve. For each coordinate iii, keep a running sum of squared gradients nin_ini​ and an adjusted gradient sum ziz_izi​; with gradient gig_igi​ on the current example:

    σi=ni+gi2−niα,zi←zi+gi−σiwi,ni←ni+gi2,wi={0∣zi∣≤λ1,−zi−sgn⁡(zi) λ1(β+ni)/α+λ2otherwise.\begin{aligned}\sigma_i&=\frac{\sqrt{n_i+g_i^2}-\sqrt{n_i}}{\alpha},\qquad z_i\leftarrow z_i+g_i-\sigma_i w_i,\qquad n_i\leftarrow n_i+g_i^2,\\ w_i&=\begin{cases}0 & |z_i|\le\lambda_1,\\[2pt] -\dfrac{z_i-\operatorname{sgn}(z_i)\,\lambda_1}{(\beta+\sqrt{n_i})/\alpha+\lambda_2} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\end{aligned}σi​wi​​=αni​+gi2​​−ni​​​,zi​←zi​+gi​−σi​wi​,ni​←ni​+gi2​,=⎩⎨⎧​0−(β+ni​​)/α+λ2​zi​−sgn(zi​)λ1​​​∣zi​∣≤λ1​,otherwise.​​

    The learning rate for coordinate iii is effectively α/(β+ni)\alpha/(\beta+\sqrt{n_i})α/(β+ni​​): rare features (small nin_ini​) take large steps, common ones small steps. The L1 threshold λ1\lambda_1λ1​ sets a weight to exactly zero until its accumulated evidence exceeds the threshold, which plain online gradient descent with L1 does not achieve. The paper's other lessons were systems lessons: encode weights in fewer bits, admit new features probabilistically, and monitor calibration per slice, because the auction multiplies the prediction by the bid (chapter 3).

    Factorization machines: a latent vector for every feature

    Factorization machines (Rendle, ICDM 2010) generalize both matrix factorization and logistic regression by modelling every pairwise feature interaction as a dot product of learned vectors, at linear cost.

    y^(x)=w0+∑i=1nwixi+∑i=1n∑j=i+1n⟨vi,vj⟩ xixj,vi∈Rk.\hat y(\mathbf x)=w_0+\sum_{i=1}^n w_ix_i+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\langle\mathbf v_i,\mathbf v_j\rangle\,x_ix_j,\qquad\mathbf v_i\in\mathbb R^k.y^​(x)=w0​+i=1∑n​wi​xi​+i=1∑n​j=i+1∑n​⟨vi​,vj​⟩xi​xj​,vi​∈Rk.

    A cross such as (user = 42, ad = 7) that never appeared in training still gets a weight, ⟨v42,v7⟩\langle\mathbf v_{42},\mathbf v_7\rangle⟨v42​,v7​⟩, learned from each feature's other co-occurrences; logistic regression on explicit crosses would give it zero. With only a user one-hot and an item one-hot as input, the FM reduces to biased matrix factorization.

    Derivation

    From O(kn2)O(kn^2)O(kn2) to O(kn)O(kn)O(kn)

    1. Sum over all ordered pairs and remove the diagonal: ∑i<j⟨vi,vj⟩xixj=12(∑i,j⟨vi,vj⟩xixj−∑i⟨vi,vi⟩xi2).\sum_{i<j}\langle\mathbf v_i,\mathbf v_j\rangle x_ix_j=\tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{i,j}\langle\mathbf v_i,\mathbf v_j\rangle x_ix_j-\sum_i\langle\mathbf v_i,\mathbf v_i\rangle x_i^2\Bigr).i<j∑​⟨vi​,vj​⟩xi​xj​=21​(i,j∑​⟨vi​,vj​⟩xi​xj​−i∑​⟨vi​,vi​⟩xi2​).
    2. Expand the dot product over the kkk factor dimensions and factor the double sum: =12∑f=1k[(∑ivi,fxi)2−∑ivi,f2xi2].=\tfrac12\sum_{f=1}^{k}\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_i v_{i,f}x_i\Bigr)^2-\sum_i v_{i,f}^2x_i^2\Bigr].=21​f=1∑k​[(i∑​vi,f​xi​)2−i∑​vi,f2​xi2​].
    3. Each inner sum touches only the nonzero xix_ixi​; with mmm nonzeros the cost is O(km)O(km)O(km).

    Check with k=1k=1k=1, v=(1,2,3)v=(1,2,3)v=(1,2,3), x=(1,1,1)x=(1,1,1)x=(1,1,1): direct sum 1⋅2+1⋅3+2⋅3=111\cdot2+1\cdot3+2\cdot3=111⋅2+1⋅3+2⋅3=11; formula 12[(1+2+3)2−(1+4+9)]=12(36−14)=11\tfrac12\bigl[(1+2+3)^2-(1+4+9)\bigr]=\tfrac12(36-14)=1121​[(1+2+3)2−(1+4+9)]=21​(36−14)=11.

    Field-aware FMs won the CTR leaderboards. Juan et al. (RecSys 2016) gave each feature one vector per field it interacts with (a user feature uses a different vector when crossing with the ad field than with the time field). Variants of FFM won the Criteo and Avazu Kaggle click-prediction challenges in 2014–2015. The cost is FFF times more parameters for FFF fields, a trade-off later deep models revisited.

    Bandits: the model only learns about what it shows

    A model trained on its own logs never sees outcomes for items it never displayed, so this era borrowed contextual bandits to trade off exploiting the best estimate against exploring uncertain ones. Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire (WWW 2010) ran LinUCB on the Yahoo! front-page news module. For each article aaa with context vector x\mathbf xx, keep a ridge regression with Aa=Da⊤Da+IA_a=D_a^{\top}D_a+IAa​=Da⊤​Da​+I and estimate θ^a=Aa−1Da⊤ca\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_a=A_a^{-1}D_a^{\top}\mathbf c_aθ^a​=Aa−1​Da⊤​ca​, where DaD_aDa​ stacks past contexts for that article and ca\mathbf c_aca​ their click outcomes; then show

    a∗=arg⁡max⁡a(x⊤θ^a+αx⊤Aa−1x).a^*=\arg\max_a\Bigl(\mathbf x^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_a+\alpha\sqrt{\mathbf x^{\top}A_a^{-1}\mathbf x}\Bigr).a∗=argamax​(x⊤θ^a​+αx⊤Aa−1​x​).

    The second term is a confidence width that shrinks as an article accumulates impressions in that region of context space. Two contributions outlived the algorithm. First, replay evaluation: with logs collected under uniformly random display, a new policy can be evaluated offline by keeping only the events where it agrees with the logged choice (Li et al., WSDM 2011); this is the root of the off-policy methods in chapter 7. Second, Chapelle and Li (NIPS 2011) showed empirically that Thompson sampling, drawing a parameter from the posterior and acting greedily on the draw, matched or beat UCB on ad and news data and was easier to implement with delayed batch updates. It became a common exploration method in ad systems.

    What broke next

    Linear models made engineers the bottleneck: every useful interaction had to be hand-specified as a feature cross. FMs learned pairwise crosses automatically but not higher-order or non-linear ones; factor models ignored the rich side information (text, images, sequences) that platforms now had. Meanwhile GPUs and the 2012 ImageNet result made deep networks practical. Era III replaced feature engineering with learned embeddings and interaction layers, and replaced the single scoring pass with a funnel.

    Era III (2013–2020): embeddings, deep ranking and the multi-stage funnel

    In this chapter

    • Draw the retrieval → ranking → re-ranking funnel and say why it exists.
    • Derive why YouTube's watch-time-weighted logistic regression predicts expected watch time.
    • Compare the explicit-interaction architectures (Wide & Deep, DeepFM, DCN, DLRM) by what they cross and at what cost.
    • Explain DIN's candidate-aware attention, two-tower retrieval with the logQ correction, and ESMM's fix for conversion-rate selection bias.
    • Summarize the reproducibility audits that deflated many neural gains.

    The gist. Deep learning entered recommendation through embeddings: every id, word and category became a learned dense vector, and neural networks learned the interactions engineers used to hand-code. Because no network can score billions of items per request, systems split into a funnel: a cheap retrieval stage (two towers whose dot product can be searched with approximate nearest neighbours) narrows millions of items to thousands, and an expensive ranking network orders those. Ranking models grew explicit cross layers, attention over each user's behaviour history and multiple task heads. A wave of reproducibility studies then showed that many published neural gains came from weak baselines, a corrective worth carrying into Era V.

    The funnel: spend compute where the decision is close

    Every large recommender since about 2016 is a cascade of increasingly expensive models over decreasing candidate sets, because exact scoring of the whole corpus with the best model is unaffordable within the latency budget.

    The design consequence is that each stage optimizes a different proxy. Retrieval is judged by recall of what the ranker would have chosen; ranking by calibrated, accurate scores on a biased candidate set; re-ranking by list-level objectives. Mismatch between stages (retrieval discarding items the ranker would love) is a persistent source of loss that Era V's generative models try to remove.

    Embeddings: ids become vectors

    The first deep idea to stick was representing each discrete entity as a learned vector, trained so that entities appearing in similar contexts get similar vectors. Microsoft's DSSM (Huang et al., CIKM 2013) mapped queries and documents through separate networks into a shared space and trained on clicks with a softmax over one clicked document and a few random ones; this is the two-tower architecture in its first form. After word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), the skip-gram objective was applied to sequences of items instead of words: purchase sequences in e-mail receipts (prod2vec, Grbovic et al., KDD 2015), item co-occurrence (item2vec, 2016), and booking sessions at Airbnb (Grbovic and Cheng, KDD 2018). Embeddings made similarity search over items cheap and transferable across tasks.

    YouTube 2016: the template for deep recommendation

    Covington, Adams and Sargin (RecSys 2016) set the template: a deep candidate generator trained as extreme multiclass classification, and a deep ranker trained to predict watch time.

    • Candidate generation treats “which video will this user watch next” as a softmax over millions of classes, P(wt=i∣U,C)=evi⊤u/∑jevj⊤uP(w_t=i\mid U,C)=e^{\mathbf v_i^{\top}\mathbf u}/\sum_j e^{\mathbf v_j^{\top}\mathbf u}P(wt​=i∣U,C)=evi⊤​u/∑j​evj⊤​u, where u\mathbf uu is the output of a network over averaged watch and search embeddings, demographics and context. Training uses sampled softmax; serving becomes a nearest-neighbour search for the largest vi⊤u\mathbf v_i^{\top}\mathbf uvi⊤​u.
    • Freshness: an “example age” feature lets the model represent how popularity depends on time since upload; at serving it is set to zero (or slightly negative), so the model does not systematically favour old content.
    • Label design: predict the next watch rather than a randomly held-out one, because viewing is sequential (episode 2 follows episode 1).
    • Ranking uses logistic regression in which each clicked impression is weighted by its watch time TiT_iTi​ and each unclicked impression has weight 1.
    Derivation

    Why the weighted odds estimate expected watch time

    Given: NNN impressions in some feature cell, kkk of them clicked with watch times T1,…,TkT_1,\dots,T_kT1​,…,Tk​; click probability P=k/NP=k/NP=k/N; expected watch time per impression E[T]=∑iTi/N\mathbb E[T]=\sum_iT_i/NE[T]=∑i​Ti​/N.

    1. A logistic regression fitted to weighted data learns odds equal to (weighted positives)/(weighted negatives) in the cell: odds=ew⊤x+b=∑i=1kTiN−k.\text{odds}=e^{\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x+b}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^kT_i}{N-k}.odds=ew⊤x+b=N−k∑i=1k​Ti​​.
    2. Divide numerator and denominator by NNN: odds=E[T]1−P≈E[T] (1+P)≈E[T]for small P.\text{odds}=\frac{\mathbb E[T]}{1-P}\approx\mathbb E[T]\,(1+P)\approx\mathbb E[T]\quad\text{for small }P.odds=1−PE[T]​≈E[T](1+P)≈E[T]for small P.

    Result: serving ew⊤x+be^{\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x+b}ew⊤x+b instead of the sigmoid ranks by approximately expected watch time.

    Check: with N=100N=100N=100, k=5k=5k=5, total watch 300 s: E[T]=3\mathbb E[T]=3E[T]=3 s, odds =300/95=3.16=300/95=3.16=300/95=3.16 s =3/(1−0.05)=3/(1-0.05)=3/(1−0.05).

    Optimizing watch time instead of clicks was a deliberate objective change (YouTube had announced in March 2012 that related and recommended videos would weight time watched more heavily) aimed at click-bait thumbnails. It also illustrates the next problem: any single engagement proxy can be gamed, which led to multi-task objectives below and to the long-term-value work in chapter 7.

    Learned feature interactions: from Wide & Deep to DLRM

    The ranking-model literature of 2016–2021 is a search for architectures that learn feature crosses an engineer would otherwise hand-code, at acceptable serving cost. Inputs are dozens to hundreds of categorical fields, each mapped to an embedding ef∈Rd\mathbf e_f\in\mathbb R^def​∈Rd, plus dense features.

    ModelOriginInteraction mechanismWhat it fixed
    Wide & DeepGoogle Play, 2016Linear model over hand-chosen cross features (wide) + MLP over embeddings (deep), trained jointlyDeep part generalizes to unseen combinations; wide part memorizes specific exceptions that an MLP over-smooths
    PNNSJTU/UCL, 2016Inner/outer products of field embeddings fed to an MLPExplicit second-order products instead of relying on the MLP to learn multiplication
    DeepFMHuawei, 2017FM layer and MLP share the same embeddingsRemoves Wide & Deep's hand-chosen crosses
    DCNGoogle, 2017Cross layers xl+1=x0xl⊤wl+bl+xl\mathbf x_{l+1}=\mathbf x_0\mathbf x_l^{\top}\mathbf w_l+\mathbf b_l+\mathbf x_lxl+1​=x0​xl⊤​wl​+bl​+xl​Bounded-degree polynomial crosses with O(d)O(d)O(d) parameters per layer
    xDeepFM, AutoInt2018, 2019Compressed interaction network; self-attention over field embeddingsVector-wise (field-level) high-order crosses
    DLRMMeta, 2019Pairwise dot products of all embeddings and a bottom-MLP output, then a top MLPA simple, systems-friendly reference; embeddings model-parallel, MLPs data-parallel
    DCN-V2Google, 2021xl+1=x0⊙(Wlxl+bl)+xl\mathbf x_{l+1}=\mathbf x_0\odot(W_l\mathbf x_l+\mathbf b_l)+\mathbf x_lxl+1​=x0​⊙(Wl​xl​+bl​)+xl​, optionally low-rankMore expressive than DCN's rank-one cross; reported in production at Google

    Why explicit crosses at all? An MLP can approximate multiplication but learns it inefficiently from sparse data; Rendle et al. (2020) showed that an MLP struggles even to learn a dot product. Each DCN layer raises the polynomial degree of the represented crosses by one, so LLL layers represent crosses of degree up to L+1L+1L+1, at a parameter cost linear in ddd for DCN and quadratic (or low-rank) for DCN-V2.

    The systems fact that shaped all of these: embeddings dominate. A model with hundreds of millions of ids per field has embedding tables of hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes while the dense layers are small. Training therefore moved from CPU parameter servers (Li et al., OSDI 2014) to GPU systems that shard embedding tables across devices and exchange looked-up rows (all-to-all) while replicating the MLPs; DLRM's paper describes exactly this hybrid parallelism, later packaged in libraries such as NVIDIA HugeCTR and Meta's TorchRec.

    Behaviour sequences: attention keyed on the candidate

    Alibaba's DIN (Zhou et al., KDD 2018) replaced the average of a user's past-behaviour embeddings with a weighted sum whose weights depend on the candidate ad, because a user's history contains many unrelated interests. For candidate ad embedding vA\mathbf v_AvA​ and history embeddings e1,…,eH\mathbf e_1,\dots,\mathbf e_He1​,…,eH​:

    vU(A)=∑j=1Ha(ej,vA) ej,\mathbf v_U(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{H}a(\mathbf e_j,\mathbf v_A)\,\mathbf e_j,vU​(A)=j=1∑H​a(ej​,vA​)ej​,

    where a(⋅)a(\cdot)a(⋅) is a small feed-forward network. The weights are deliberately not softmax-normalized, so a user with many relevant behaviours produces a larger vector than one with a single weak match. Someone who bought a swimsuit and a laptop bag is represented differently when the candidate is goggles than when it is a mouse. The line continued with DIEN (AAAI 2019: a GRU models how interests evolve) and SIM (CIKM 2020: first retrieve the relevant subset of a very long, lifelong behaviour sequence, then attend over that subset), which pushed usable history from hundreds of events to tens of thousands (up to about 54,000).

    In parallel, session-based recommenders borrowed language-model architectures. GRU4Rec (Hidasi et al., ICLR 2016) predicted the next click in a session with a recurrent network; SASRec (Kang and McAuley, ICDM 2018) used causal self-attention; BERT4Rec (Sun et al., CIKM 2019) used a bidirectional masked objective. Replication then complicated the ranking. Petrov and Macdonald (RecSys 2022) found published BERT4Rec-versus-SASRec comparisons inconsistent: BERT4Rec needs up to 30 times longer training, many later papers used an under-trained version, and properly trained it does beat SASRec. Klenitskiy and Vasilev (RecSys 2023) then showed that SASRec trained with a full-softmax cross-entropy loss, instead of its original sampled binary loss, outperforms BERT4Rec. Loss and training budget mattered as much as architecture. Sequence modelling returned at a far larger scale in Era V.

    Two-tower retrieval and the logQ correction

    Retrieval models score a user and an item with separate networks and a dot product, so item vectors can be precomputed and searched with approximate nearest neighbours; training them with in-batch negatives requires a correction for popularity. Write s(x,y)=u(x)⊤v(y)s(x,y)=\mathbf u(x)^{\top}\mathbf v(y)s(x,y)=u(x)⊤v(y). The ideal loss is a softmax over the whole corpus, which is unaffordable. Using the other items in a training batch as negatives is cheap, but items appear in batches in proportion to their frequency pjp_jpj​, so popular items are over-represented as negatives and get pushed down too far. Yi et al. (RecSys 2019, YouTube) subtract the log sampling probability from each logit during training:

    sc(x,yj)=s(x,yj)−log⁡pj,L=−log⁡esc(x,yi)∑j∈batchesc(x,yj).s^c(x,y_j)=s(x,y_j)-\log p_j,\qquad \mathcal L=-\log\frac{e^{s^c(x,y_i)}}{\sum_{j\in\text{batch}}e^{s^c(x,y_j)}}.sc(x,yj​)=s(x,yj​)−logpj​,L=−log∑j∈batch​esc(x,yj​)esc(x,yi​)​.

    This is the standard importance-sampling correction for sampled softmax: dividing each sampled term by its proposal probability makes the batch sum an estimate of the full-corpus normalizer. The paper estimates pjp_jpj​ on the fly from a stream of item ids by tracking the average gap between successive occurrences of each item. At serving time the raw score s(x,y)s(x,y)s(x,y) is used.

    Approximate nearest-neighbour search made retrieval over billions of vectors practical. Product quantization (Jégou, Douze and Schmid, 2011) compresses vectors into short codes with fast distance tables; HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016) builds a navigable multi-layer proximity graph with logarithmic-like search; FAISS (Johnson, Douze and Jégou, 2017) put both on GPUs; ScaNN (Guo et al., ICML 2020) quantizes with a loss aimed at preserving inner products rather than distances. Facebook's embedding-based retrieval for search (Huang et al., KDD 2020) is a candid production account, including the finding that random negatives beat negatives drawn from impressed-but-not-clicked results for retrieval, because retrieval must separate relevant from irrelevant rather than good from slightly better. Graph models such as Pinterest's PinSage (Ying et al., KDD 2018), a graph convolutional network over a pin–board graph with billions of nodes, and LightGCN (He et al., SIGIR 2020) supplied retrieval embeddings from the interaction graph.

    Multi-task ranking: one model, several outcomes

    Ranking models moved from predicting one outcome to predicting several (click, like, share, watch time, conversion) with shared lower layers, and two papers in 2018 defined the patterns.

    ESMM fixes conversion-rate selection bias by never training CVR on clicks alone. Conversion is observed only after a click, so a CVR model trained on clicked impressions learns P(conv∣click,x)P(\text{conv}\mid\text{click},x)P(conv∣click,x) from a sample that differs from the impressions it must score, and has few positives. Ma et al. (SIGIR 2018, Alibaba) model over all impressions:

    P(click∧conv∣x)⏟pCTCVR=P(click∣x)⏟pCTR×P(conv∣click,x)⏟pCVR,\underbrace{P(\text{click}\wedge\text{conv}\mid x)}_{\text{pCTCVR}}=\underbrace{P(\text{click}\mid x)}_{\text{pCTR}}\times\underbrace{P(\text{conv}\mid\text{click},x)}_{\text{pCVR}},pCTCVRP(click∧conv∣x)​​=pCTRP(click∣x)​​×pCVRP(conv∣click,x)​​,

    with losses on pCTR (label: click) and pCTCVR (label: click and conversion), both defined on every impression. The pCVR tower receives gradients only through the product, and shares embeddings with the data-rich CTR task.

    MMoE lets tasks share experts with learned, per-task mixing. Ma et al. (KDD 2018, Google) use nnn expert networks fif_ifi​ and a softmax gate per task kkk:

    yk=hk(∑i=1ngk(x)i fi(x)),gk(x)=softmax⁡(Wgkx).y_k=h^k\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}g^k(x)_i\,f_i(x)\Bigr),\qquad g^k(x)=\operatorname{softmax}(W_{g_k}x).yk​=hk(i=1∑n​gk(x)i​fi​(x)),gk(x)=softmax(Wgk​​x).

    Weakly related tasks can use different experts, which reduces the negative transfer of a single shared bottom. YouTube's 2019 ranking system (Zhao et al., RecSys 2019) combined MMoE with a shallow “position tower” to absorb position bias (chapter 7); Tencent's PLE (Tang et al., RecSys 2020) separated shared and task-specific experts. Final ranking typically combines task predictions with a hand-tuned or learned formula, which is where product policy enters the model.

    The reproducibility crisis: many neural gains were weak baselines

    Several audits from 2019 to 2022 found that a large share of published neural recommendation gains disappeared against properly tuned classical baselines.

    • Dacrema, Cremonesi and Jannach (RecSys 2019) tried to reproduce 18 neural methods from top venues; only 7 could be reproduced with reasonable effort, and 6 of those were often beaten by simple, well-tuned neighbourhood or linear methods.
    • Rendle, Krichene, Zhang and Anderson (RecSys 2020) revisited neural collaborative filtering (He et al., WWW 2017): a carefully tuned dot-product model beat the learned MLP similarity, and an MLP needed large capacity to approximate a dot product.
    • Krichene and Rendle (KDD 2020) showed that evaluating against a small sample of random negatives, a common shortcut, can reverse the ranking of methods relative to full-corpus metrics.

    How to read industrial results after this

    Industrial papers report online A/B gains on internal baselines, which cannot be audited. They remain the best available evidence of what worked at that company, but treat “+X% engagement” as conditional on an unknown baseline, unknown metric definition and unknown duration. The same caution applies, more strongly, to Era V claims in chapter 8.

    What broke next

    The deep stack worked, but three problems were left: models trained on their own biased logs; a pricing layer still built for manual bidders; and, from 2017, regulators and platform owners cutting off the cross-site identity signal these models consumed. Chapter 6 follows the ad-pricing changes; chapter 7 covers bias, causality and privacy.

    The ads track (2007–2026): exchanges, first-price auctions and autobidding

    In this chapter

    • Trace how pricing moved from the advertiser's CPC bid to the platform bidding on the advertiser's behalf for conversions.
    • Derive the budget-paced bid v/(1+μ)v/(1+\mu)v/(1+μ) in a second-price auction and the dual update that finds μ\muμ.
    • Explain why display advertising moved to first-price auctions in 2017–2019, and derive optimal bid shading against a known competing-bid distribution.
    • Derive why a target-CPA autobidder bids a uniform multiple of value, sometimes above value.
    • Name what advertisers gave up in exchange for campaign automation (Performance Max, Advantage+).

    The gist. In 2005 an advertiser chose keywords and typed a bid per click. By 2025 the advertiser typically states a budget and a target cost per conversion or return on ad spend, uploads creative assets, and the platform's models choose the audience, placement, creative and the bid for each impression. Three changes drove this: real-time exchanges that priced each impression separately; prediction good enough that the platform could take on conversion risk (oCPM, oCPC); and a move from second-price to first-price auctions that made manual bidding even harder. The algorithms are constrained optimization: each bid is predicted value scaled by a multiplier that enforces the advertiser's budget or target.

    Exchanges and real-time bidding: price every impression

    From about 2009, display inventory was increasingly sold impression by impression in real-time auctions, which turned buying into a per-impression prediction problem for the buyer. Ad exchanges (Right Media, bought by Yahoo in 2007; DoubleClick's AdX, which Google acquired with DoubleClick in 2008) let publishers offer each impression to many buyers. Demand-side platforms (DSPs) bid on the advertiser's behalf, typically within about 100 milliseconds. The OpenRTB project (started in late 2010; version 2.0 adopted by the IAB in January 2012) standardized the bid request and response (sources). A DSP's bid for an impression is its estimate of the advertiser's value: for a CPA goal, predicted conversion probability times the target cost per acquisition. Most exchanges initially ran second-price auctions, under which bidding true value is the textbook advice.

    Per-impression buying created new modelling problems for the buyer. The buyer must predict the probability of a conversion, the distribution of the highest competing bid (the bid landscape), and how quickly its budget will be spent. Zhang, Yuan and Wang (KDD 2014) derived optimal bidding functions under a budget given a winning-probability curve and found them concave in predicted value rather than linear, a consequence of the budget constraint combined with a concave winning-probability curve (without a budget the optimal bid is linear in value).

    The platform takes on conversion risk: oCPM and oCPC

    Once conversion prediction was reliable, platforms let advertisers bid for conversions while still allocating impressions by expected value, and the auction score became bid × pCTR × pCVR. Under optimized CPM (Facebook, from 2012), the advertiser states a value per conversion; the platform converts it into an impression bid with its own models and charges per impression. Under optimized CPC (Alibaba's oCPC, Zhu et al., KDD 2017), the advertiser sets a CPC bid and the system adjusts it up or down within a bounded range according to predicted conversion rate. In both, the ranking score for an ad with conversion target aaa (dollars per conversion) is

    eCPM=1000×a×pCTR×pCVR(+ quality terms),\text{eCPM}=1000\times a\times\text{pCTR}\times\text{pCVR}\quad(+\ \text{quality terms}),eCPM=1000×a×pCTR×pCVR(+ quality terms),

    where pCVR here is conversions per click. Meta's public description of its auction ranks by “total value”: the advertiser's bid times the estimated action rate, plus an ad-quality term, so a lower bid with a better predicted response can win. Errors in pCTR or pCVR now move money directly: an inflated pCVR overbids on the advertiser's behalf. This is why the ESMM-style conversion models of chapter 5 and the delayed-feedback corrections of chapter 7 were built by ad teams.

    Budgets and pacing: one multiplier per campaign

    Under a daily budget, the optimal bid in a truthful auction is value divided by 1+μ1+\mu1+μ, where μ\muμ is the budget constraint's shadow price; pacing algorithms estimate μ\muμ online. Suppose a campaign faces impressions i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,ni=1,…,n with values viv_ivi​ and second-price costs pip_ipi​, and chooses which to win, xi∈{0,1}x_i\in\{0,1\}xi​∈{0,1}, to maximize surplus subject to spending at most BBB:

    Derivation

    Budget-paced bidding

    1. Lagrangian with multiplier μ≥0\mu\ge0μ≥0: ∑ixi(vi−pi)−μ(∑ixipi−B)=∑ixi(vi−(1+μ)pi)+μB.\sum_i x_i(v_i-p_i)-\mu\Bigl(\sum_ix_ip_i-B\Bigr)=\sum_ix_i\bigl(v_i-(1+\mu)p_i\bigr)+\mu B.i∑​xi​(vi​−pi​)−μ(i∑​xi​pi​−B)=i∑​xi​(vi​−(1+μ)pi​)+μB.
    2. For fixed μ\muμ, win impression iii exactly when pi≤vi/(1+μ)p_i\le v_i/(1+\mu)pi​≤vi​/(1+μ).
    3. In a second-price auction you pay pip_ipi​, the highest competing bid, and win when your bid exceeds it, so bidding bi=vi/(1+μ)b_i=v_i/(1+\mu)bi​=vi​/(1+μ) implements step 2.
    4. Choose μ\muμ so that expected spend equals BBB if the budget binds; μ=0\mu=0μ=0 otherwise.

    Result: one scalar per campaign shades all bids proportionally.

    Scope: this is exact for the linear relaxation, where fractions of impressions can be bought; with indivisible impressions it is optimal up to one marginal impression (exercise D4 leaves $2 unspent). Check: with an unlimited budget, μ=0\mu=0μ=0 and the bid is the value, the textbook second-price answer. As the budget shrinks, μ\muμ rises and only the impressions with the highest value-to-price ratio are bought.

    Online, μ\muμ is updated by a dual gradient step after each period ttt: μ←max⁡{0, μ+η (spendt−B/T)}\mu\leftarrow\max\{0,\ \mu+\eta\,(\text{spend}_t-B/T)\}μ←max{0, μ+η(spendt​−B/T)}, raising it when spend runs ahead of the per-period target. Balseiro and Gur (Management Science, 2019) analyse this adaptive pacing and prove regret guarantees. Production pacing also uses throttling, entering only a random fraction of auctions (LinkedIn, Agarwal et al., KDD 2014; Yahoo's smart pacing, Xu et al., KDD 2015), which is simpler but discards the value ranking that bid shading preserves.

    Display moves to first price: why, and how to shade

    Between 2017 and 2019 most of programmatic display moved from second-price to first-price auctions, because chains of auctions had made “second price” opaque and manipulable. Header bidding (from about 2014–2015, with the open-source Prebid.js wrapper) let publishers solicit bids from several exchanges at once before calling their ad server, so an impression passed through several auctions in sequence. Second-price rules lose their meaning in a chain: exchanges used undisclosed floors, and the price paid depended on which auction cleared it. Exchanges moved to first price, where the rule is simple (pay your bid); Google Ad Manager announced its move to a unified first-price auction in March 2019 and completed it that September. Buyers responded with bid shading, bidding below value by an amount estimated from the competition.

    Against a known distribution of competing bids, the optimal first-price bid balances a higher margin against a lower win rate. Let the highest competing bid ZZZ have CDF FFF and density fff. Expected surplus is U(b)=(v−b)F(b)U(b)=(v-b)F(b)U(b)=(v−b)F(b); setting U′(b)=0U'(b)=0U′(b)=0 gives

    v−b∗=F(b∗)f(b∗).v-b^*=\frac{F(b^*)}{f(b^*)}.v−b∗=f(b∗)F(b∗)​.

    With Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L), F(b)/f(b)=bF(b)/f(b)=bF(b)/f(b)=b, so b∗=v/2b^*=v/2b∗=v/2.

    In practice FFF is unknown and depends on the impression; shading models estimate it from win/loss logs, which are censored (a loss reveals only that the winning price exceeded your bid, and some exchanges report the minimum bid needed to win). This is a survival-analysis problem, and an example of how a market-design change creates a new prediction task.

    Autobidding: the platform bids to the advertiser's target

    Target-CPA and target-ROAS bidding make the platform maximize conversions or conversion value subject to the advertiser's cost constraint, and in a truthful auction the optimal policy is to bid a uniform multiple of each impression's value. Google's Smart Bidding, Meta's cost-cap and value-optimization bidding and similar products all fit one model, analysed by Aggarwal, Badanidiyuru and Mehta (WINE 2019). Let viv_ivi​ be the value of impression iii in dollars (predicted conversions times target CPA, or predicted conversion value divided by target ROAS):

    Derivation

    Uniform bid scaling for a value maximizer

    Problem: maximize ∑ixivi\sum_ix_iv_i∑i​xi​vi​ subject to the target ∑ixipi≤∑ixivi\sum_ix_ip_i\le\sum_ix_iv_i∑i​xi​pi​≤∑i​xi​vi​ (average cost per value at most 1) and the budget ∑ixipi≤B\sum_ix_ip_i\le B∑i​xi​pi​≤B.

    1. Lagrangian with λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0 for the target and μ≥0\mu\ge0μ≥0 for the budget: ∑ixi[(1+λ)vi−(λ+μ)pi]+μB.\sum_ix_i\bigl[(1+\lambda)v_i-(\lambda+\mu)p_i\bigr]+\mu B.i∑​xi​[(1+λ)vi​−(λ+μ)pi​]+μB.
    2. Win impression iii exactly when pi≤κvip_i\le\kappa v_ipi​≤κvi​ with κ=1+λλ+μ\kappa=\dfrac{1+\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}κ=λ+μ1+λ​.
    3. In a truthful auction that is implemented by bidding bi=κvib_i=\kappa v_ibi​=κvi​, one multiplier for the whole campaign.
    4. If only the target binds (μ=0\mu=0μ=0), κ=(1+λ)/λ>1\kappa=(1+\lambda)/\lambda>1κ=(1+λ)/λ>1: the bidder bids above value on every impression.

    Result: autobidding is value prediction times one learned multiplier; with a target and slack budget, the multiplier exceeds one. As with pacing, exact for the linear relaxation.

    Check: overbidding is consistent with the target because the constraint is on the average. Cheap impressions bought far below value create slack that pays for expensive ones bought above value. A profit maximizer (surplus objective, as in the pacing derivation) never bids above value; a value maximizer with an average-cost target does.

    The same paper shows that when all bidders are such value maximizers, the VCG auction's welfare (measured as “liquid welfare”) is at least half the optimum, a price of anarchy of 2. This is a named result, not proved here. The practical consequence: as autobidders came to dominate, auction design research shifted from profit-maximizing bidders to value maximizers with return-on-spend constraints, and reserve prices and boosts were re-derived for that model.

    Campaign automation: the platform chooses almost everything

    From 2021 the largest platforms bundled targeting, placement, creative selection and bidding into single automated products, so the advertiser's inputs shrank to a goal, a budget, assets and a conversion feed. Google's Performance Max (generally available in November 2021) runs one campaign across Search, YouTube, Display, Discover, Gmail and Maps; Meta's Advantage+ shopping campaigns (August 2022) automate audience and placement; AppLovin's AXON 2.0 (second quarter of 2023) drove a large rise in AppLovin's reported advertising revenue on mobile-game inventory (sources). Generative tools that produce or vary ad images and text were added to these products from 2023.

    Why automation won

    The platform sees cross-advertiser data the advertiser cannot: competing bids, user responses across campaigns, inventory forecasts. After ATT (chapter 7) removed much of the user-level signal advertisers used for their own targeting, broad automated targeting driven by the platform's models often performed as well or better.

    What the advertiser gave up

    Control and visibility: placement-level reporting, keyword control and exclusion levers were reduced. The platform both sets the bid and grades the result with its own attribution, a principal–agent problem. Advertisers' only independent check is a randomized incrementality test, which the platform also often runs.

    Inference. The steady direction is that the advertiser specifies an objective and the platform owns the optimization. That raises the value of the platform's predictive models and lowers the value of advertiser-side tooling; it also concentrates measurement in the party that is paid. The open question for 2026 is how ads are priced and measured in conversational AI answers, where there is no ranked list of slots to auction (chapter 8).

    Cross-cutting (2002–2025): feedback loops, causality and the privacy shock

    In this chapter

    • Explain why a recommender trained on its own logs learns its own biases, and name the main ones (position, exposure, selection, popularity).
    • Correct position bias with inverse propensity weighting, and evaluate a new policy from old logs with IPS and doubly robust estimators.
    • Write Chapelle's delayed-feedback likelihood for conversions.
    • Explain why attributed conversions overstate what ads cause, and what randomized lift tests measure instead.
    • Date the privacy shocks (ITP, GDPR, ATT, Privacy Sandbox) and say what each removed from the models' inputs.

    The gist. Every log a recommender learns from was produced by an earlier version of the same recommender, so the data record what was shown, where, and to whom, not what people would have chosen. Clicks on the top slot reflect the slot as much as the item; items never shown never get labels; ads get credit for purchases that would have happened anyway. From about 2016 the field borrowed tools from causal inference: propensity weighting, off-policy estimators and randomized holdouts. Then, from 2017, browsers, regulators and Apple removed much of the cross-site and cross-app identity these models consumed, forcing ad systems to learn from aggregated, delayed and noisier signals.

    The data are generated by the policy

    Logged interactions are outcomes of the deployed policy's choices, so naive training on them confounds item quality with exposure. Four biases recur:

    • Position bias. Users click higher positions more regardless of relevance.
    • Exposure (selection) bias. Labels exist only for shown items; for ratings, users choose what to rate, so missing ratings are not missing at random (Schnabel et al., ICML 2016, treated recommendations as treatments and corrected with propensities).
    • Popularity bias and feedback loops. Popular items are shown more, collect more positive labels, and are shown even more. Simulations by Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt (RecSys 2018) show this algorithmic confounding homogenizes what users see without improving utility.
    • Conversion selection bias. Conversions are observed only after clicks (addressed by ESMM in chapter 5).

    Position bias and inverse propensity weighting

    Under the examination hypothesis, a click requires that the user examines the position and finds the item relevant; dividing each click by the examination probability of its position removes position bias in expectation. Write P(click∣i,k)=θk⋅γiP(\text{click}\mid i,k)=\theta_k\cdot\gamma_iP(click∣i,k)=θk​⋅γi​, where θk\theta_kθk​ is the probability that position kkk is examined and γi\gamma_iγi​ the probability that item iii is clicked when examined. Joachims (KDD 2002) first trained rankers from click logs; Craswell et al. (WSDM 2008) proposed the cascade model, in which users scan down and stop at the first satisfying result; Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel (WSDM 2017) gave the propensity-weighted, unbiased learning-to-rank estimator.

    Worked example

    Two items, two positions

    Given: examination probabilities θ1=1.0\theta_1=1.0θ1​=1.0, θ3=0.4\theta_3=0.4θ3​=0.4. Item A was shown 1,000 times at position 1 and got 100 clicks; item B was shown 1,000 times at position 3 and got 40 clicks.

    1. Naive CTR: A =0.10=0.10=0.10, B =0.04=0.04=0.04. A looks 2.5 times better.
    2. IPS-weighted clicks: A =100/1.0=100=100/1.0=100=100/1.0=100; B =40/0.4=100=40/0.4=100=40/0.4=100.
    3. Estimated relevance γ^\hat\gammaγ^​: A =100/1,000=0.10=100/1{,}000=0.10=100/1,000=0.10, B =100/1,000=0.10=100/1{,}000=0.10=100/1,000=0.10.

    Result: after correction the two items are equally relevant; the naive model would have kept B at position 3 for ever.

    Check: E[clicksB]=1,000 θ3γB=1,000×0.4×0.10=40\mathbb E[\text{clicks}_B]=1{,}000\,\theta_3\gamma_B=1{,}000\times0.4\times0.10=40E[clicksB​]=1,000θ3​γB​=1,000×0.4×0.10=40, matching the data.

    The propensities must themselves be estimated: by randomizing positions for a small slice of traffic (costly), by swapping adjacent results, or by an EM algorithm over regular logs (Wang et al., WSDM 2018). Deep rankers often take a different route: feed position as an input to a separate shallow “bias tower” during training and drop it at serving (YouTube, Zhao et al., RecSys 2019; Huawei's PAL, Guo et al., RecSys 2019), so the main network learns γ\gammaγ while the bias tower absorbs θ\thetaθ.

    Off-policy evaluation and learning

    Logs from a randomized (or at least stochastic) policy let you estimate how a different policy would have performed, by reweighting each logged reward by the ratio of the two policies' action probabilities. If the logging policy μ\muμ chose action aia_iai​ in context xix_ixi​ and observed reward rir_iri​, the inverse-propensity-score estimate of a new policy π\piπ's value is

    V^IPS(π)=1n∑i=1nri π(ai∣xi)μ(ai∣xi),\hat V_{\text{IPS}}(\pi)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\,\frac{\pi(a_i\mid x_i)}{\mu(a_i\mid x_i)},V^IPS​(π)=n1​i=1∑n​ri​μ(ai​∣xi​)π(ai​∣xi​)​,

    unbiased whenever μ(a∣x)>0\mu(a\mid x)>0μ(a∣x)>0 wherever π(a∣x)>0\pi(a\mid x)>0π(a∣x)>0. Its variance explodes when the policies differ, so practice clips the weights (trading bias for variance) or uses the doubly robust estimator (Dudík, Langford and Li, ICML 2011), which adds a reward model r^\hat rr^ and uses IPS only to correct the model's residual:

    V^DR(π)=1n∑i=1n[∑aπ(a∣xi) r^(xi,a)+π(ai∣xi)μ(ai∣xi)(ri−r^(xi,ai))].\hat V_{\text{DR}}(\pi)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\Bigl[\sum_a\pi(a\mid x_i)\,\hat r(x_i,a)+\frac{\pi(a_i\mid x_i)}{\mu(a_i\mid x_i)}\bigl(r_i-\hat r(x_i,a_i)\bigr)\Bigr].V^DR​(π)=n1​i=1∑n​[a∑​π(a∣xi​)r^(xi​,a)+μ(ai​∣xi​)π(ai​∣xi​)​(ri​−r^(xi​,ai​))].

    It is unbiased if either the propensities or the reward model is correct. Bottou et al. (JMLR 2013) applied counterfactual reasoning to Bing's ad placement, estimating the effect of changes to the auction and the ad-load policy from logs with randomized perturbations. Swaminathan and Joachims (ICML 2015) turned evaluation into learning (counterfactual risk minimization, with a variance penalty).

    YouTube's REINFORCE recommender (Chen et al., WSDM 2019) brought off-policy correction to a production policy-gradient system. The gradient of the policy's expected reward is reweighted by πθ(a∣s)/β(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a\mid s)/\beta(a\mid s)πθ​(a∣s)/β(a∣s), with β\betaβ the logging policy, itself estimated by a separate head because the logs mixed many earlier systems. Because the system recommends KKK items at once, the paper derives a top-KKK correction that multiplies the gradient by

    λK(s,a)=K(1−πθ(a∣s))K−1,\lambda_K(s,a)=K\bigl(1-\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\bigr)^{K-1},λK​(s,a)=K(1−πθ​(a∣s))K−1,

    which shrinks the push on items the policy already ranks with high probability (they will appear in the top KKK anyway) and boosts it for items with small probability.

    The objective keeps moving: clicks, watch time, satisfaction

    Each engagement proxy was adopted to fix the previous one's failure and then showed its own. Click optimization rewarded misleading thumbnails; YouTube began weighting recommendations by time watched in March 2012 and extended this to search that October. Watch time rewards long, compulsive viewing; platforms added survey-based satisfaction labels and “valued” engagement as additional ranking targets. Facebook announced a re-weighting toward “meaningful social interactions” among friends and family in January 2018. In ads, the analogous move went from clicks to conversions to conversion value (chapter 6). The common structure is a multi-task model whose heads are combined by a weighting formula, the place where product policy is set; the algorithms of chapter 5 do not choose the weights.

    Delayed feedback: conversions arrive late

    Conversions can arrive days after the click, so a recent unconverted click is not yet a negative; Chapelle (KDD 2014) modelled the conversion and its delay jointly. Let p(x)p(x)p(x) be the probability of eventual conversion and assume the delay DDD given conversion is exponential with rate λ(x)\lambda(x)λ(x). For a click observed for elapsed time eee:

    P(converted at delay d∣x)=p(x) λ(x) e−λ(x)d,P(no conversion yet∣x,e)=1−p(x)+p(x) e−λ(x)e.\begin{aligned}P(\text{converted at delay }d\mid x)&=p(x)\,\lambda(x)\,e^{-\lambda(x)d},\\ P(\text{no conversion yet}\mid x,e)&=1-p(x)+p(x)\,e^{-\lambda(x)e}.\end{aligned}P(converted at delay d∣x)P(no conversion yet∣x,e)​=p(x)λ(x)e−λ(x)d,=1−p(x)+p(x)e−λ(x)e.​

    The second line is the key: a click that has waited only an hour contributes little evidence against conversion, one that has waited thirty days contributes almost full evidence. Training on “converted so far” labels would bias p(x)p(x)p(x) downward, most strongly for new campaigns, exactly the ones whose bids depend on it. Later work replaced the exponential assumption with non-parametric delay models and importance weighting for streaming training.

    Attribution versus incrementality

    Attribution credits an ad for conversions that follow it; incrementality is the number of conversions the ad caused, and only randomized experiments measure it reliably. Lewis and Rao (QJE 2015) showed that ad effects are so small relative to the variance of individual purchases that even very large experiments have little power, the “unfavorable economics” of measuring returns. Johnson, Lewis and Nubbemeyer (JMR 2017) introduced ghost ads: log, in the control group, the ads that would have been shown, so treatment and control are compared on the comparable subset and the experiment is far more precise. Gordon et al. (Marketing Science 2019) ran 15 large Facebook experiments and found that observational methods, even with rich covariates, often failed to recover the experimental lift, frequently overstating it. For model builders this means the label the ad system optimizes (attributed conversion) is not the quantity the advertiser should pay for (incremental conversion), a gap that uplift models, which rank by predicted treatment effect rather than predicted outcome, try to close.

    The privacy shock, 2017–2025

    Between 2017 and 2021 browsers, regulators and Apple removed most cross-site and cross-app user identifiers from advertising, and the industry's response changed what ad models learn from.

    1. Sep 2017
      Safari Intelligent Tracking Prevention (Safari 11) restricts third-party cookies with a classifier for tracking domains; Firefox enabled Enhanced Tracking Protection by default in 2019.
    2. Mar 2018
      SKAdNetwork arrives in iOS 11.3: Apple-mediated, aggregated install attribution with no user-level identifier. Later versions add a small conversion value, delayed postbacks and, in SKAdNetwork 4 (2022), multiple postbacks with crowd-size thresholds.
    3. May 2018
      GDPR becomes enforceable in the EU: consent and lawful-basis rules for personal data, including advertising identifiers. California's CCPA follows in January 2020.
    4. Aug 2019
      Google announces the Privacy Sandbox for Chrome: replace third-party cookies with on-device APIs (FLoC, later Topics; FLEDGE, later Protected Audience; Attribution Reporting with noise).
    5. Apr 2021
      App Tracking Transparency enforced from iOS 14.5: apps must ask permission to track users across other companies' apps and sites; the advertising identifier (IDFA) is zeroed unless the user opts in.
    6. Feb 2022
      Meta tells investors ATT will cost it about $10 billion of 2022 revenue Call.
    7. Jul 2024
      Google abandons third-party cookie deprecation in Chrome in favour of user choice; in April 2025 it drops even a standalone choice prompt.
    8. Oct 2025
      Google retires most Privacy Sandbox technologies, including Topics, Protected Audience and Attribution Reporting, citing low adoption; a few (CHIPS, FedCM, Private State Tokens) remain.

    What changed in the models. On iOS, an ad network lost the user-level label linking an ad impression in one app to an install or purchase in another. Responses, roughly in order of adoption:

    • Server-side and first-party signals. Advertisers send conversions from their own servers (Meta's Conversions API, Google's enhanced conversions), matched on hashed first-party identifiers such as e-mail where users consented.
