    • Modelled conversions. Platforms estimate the conversions they can no longer observe and report them alongside observed ones; the reported number becomes partly a model output.
    • Learning from aggregated labels. Training from postbacks that report counts per campaign with delay and noise, rather than per-impression labels; calibration at the aggregate level replaces per-user validation.
    • Contextual and on-platform signals. More weight on what the platform observes itself: in-app behaviour, the content being viewed, device and context features.

    Inference. The privacy shock rewarded scale of first-party data and model capacity: platforms that observe both the ad exposure and the conversion inside their own surfaces (a marketplace, a closed app ecosystem, a game network with its own measurement partner) lost less signal, and the general advertising models of chapter 8 were partly a response to sparser, noisier labels. The Privacy Sandbox's retirement in 2025 left Chrome with third-party cookies still available and no standard privacy-preserving replacement in place.

    Era V (2021–2026): scaling laws and generative recommenders

    In this chapter

    • Explain why DLRM-style models stopped improving with more parameters, and what changed to restore scaling.
    • Build a semantic ID with residual quantization and explain generative retrieval (TIGER).
    • Describe the HSTU reformulation of ranking and retrieval as sequential transduction, and its reported scale.
    • Separate what is published about 2024–2025 production systems (OneRec, Andromeda, GEM, Netflix's foundation model) from what is only claimed.
    • Name the open problems for ads in conversational AI answers.

    The gist. By the early 2020s, ranking models had grown mostly by adding embedding rows, which raised memory but not quality much. Two ideas changed the slope. First, treat a user's history as a long sequence of actions and train a Transformer-like model to predict the next action, as language models predict the next token; at Meta this produced quality that kept improving with compute across three orders of magnitude. Second, give items short token codes (semantic IDs) built from their content, so a model can generate the next item's code directly instead of searching for it. In 2025 Kuaishou reported an end-to-end generative pipeline in production, and Meta described large foundation ad models whose knowledge is transferred into serving models. Most of the evidence is from the companies themselves.

    Did recommendation models scale? Not by adding embedding rows

    Through about 2022 most growth in recommender parameter counts was embedding tables, and quality gains from more parameters were small; the compute spent per example stayed modest. Systems papers advertised trillions of parameters (Kuaishou and ETH's Persia, 2021, trained up to 100 trillion), but almost all of them sit in sparse lookups, each example touching only a few. Ardalani et al. (Meta, 2022) studied scaling laws for DLRM-style models and found that growing data improved quality more efficiently than growing parameters, with parameter scaling showing diminishing returns. The interaction and MLP layers, where compute per example is spent, were tiny by language-model standards.

    The 2024 answer was to spend compute on interactions and sequences. Meta's Wukong (Zhang et al., ICML 2024) stacked factorization-machine-style interaction blocks and reported a scaling law across two orders of magnitude of model complexity, beyond 100 GFLOP per example, on internal data Paper. The larger departure was HSTU, below.

    Freshness kept mattering

    Scale did not remove the need for fresh models. ByteDance's Monolith (Liu et al., 2022) described the training system behind real-time recommendation: a collisionless embedding table based on cuckoo hashing (no hash collisions between ids), expiring embeddings for stale ids, frequency filtering for rare ones, and online training that pushes sparse parameters to serving every few minutes while dense parameters sync daily Paper. It answers the same freshness problem Facebook measured in 2014 (chapter 4).

    Semantic IDs and generative retrieval

    Generative retrieval replaces nearest-neighbour search with decoding: the model outputs a short code that identifies the next item, and codes are built so that similar items share prefixes. Google's TIGER (Rajput et al., NeurIPS 2023) builds a semantic ID for each item from a content embedding z\mathbf zz (from a text encoder over the item's metadata) by residual quantization: with mmm codebooks {ec(l)}\{\mathbf e^{(l)}_c\}{ec(l)​},

    r0=z,cl=arg⁡min⁡c∥rl−ec(l)∥,rl+1=rl−ecl(l),l=0,…,m−1.\mathbf r_0=\mathbf z,\qquad c_l=\arg\min_c\bigl\lVert\mathbf r_l-\mathbf e^{(l)}_c\bigr\rVert,\qquad \mathbf r_{l+1}=\mathbf r_l-\mathbf e^{(l)}_{c_l},\qquad l=0,\dots,m-1.r0​=z,cl​=argcmin​​rl​−ec(l)​​,rl+1​=rl​−ecl​(l)​,l=0,…,m−1.

    The item's ID is the tuple (c0,c1,…,cm−1)(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{m-1})(c0​,c1​,…,cm−1​): c0c_0c0​ encodes the coarse region of embedding space, each later code refines the residual. The codebooks and encoder are learned jointly as an RQ-VAE; TIGER used three levels of 256 codes plus an extra token to separate items that collide. A sequence-to-sequence Transformer reads the user's history as a sequence of semantic-ID tokens and decodes the next item's tokens with beam search.

    Worked example

    Why semantic IDs help cold start and memory

    Given: three levels of 256 codes each.

    1. Addressable IDs: 2563=16,777,216256^3=16{,}777{,}2162563=16,777,216 distinct tuples.
    2. Output vocabulary the decoder needs: 3×256=7683\times256=7683×256=768 token embeddings (one table per level), instead of one row per item (1,024 counting TIGER's extra collision code).
    3. A new item gets a semantic ID from its content embedding immediately; if it lands next to popular items in content space it shares their prefix, so the model can generate it before it has any interactions.

    Result: 16.8 million addressable items with 768 output embeddings, and an ID for a new item on day zero.

    Check: the trade-off is the inverse. Two items with similar content but different audiences share a prefix and must be told apart by later codes, so semantic IDs alone memorize less than one free embedding per item. YouTube's ranking study (Singh et al., RecSys 2024) found semantic-ID features generalized better on new and long-tail items while matching random-ID memorization overall.

    Earlier, P5 (Geng et al., RecSys 2022) had cast several recommendation tasks as text-to-text prompts for one language model, and zero-shot LLM rankers showed that general language models know something about item similarity. Neither ran at production latency; semantic IDs were the bridge that made generation over a catalogue tractable.

    HSTU: recommendation as sequential transduction

    Meta's HSTU (Zhai et al., ICML 2024) recast both retrieval and ranking as predicting the next element of a user's chronological stream of (item, action) events, and reported that quality improved as a power law of training compute over three orders of magnitude. The paper's title, “Actions speak louder than words”, states the premise: the data are not text but actions, and a recommendation model should be trained like a language model on them. Key elements:

    • Reformulation. Heterogeneous features (demographics, counters, context) are folded into the sequence as tokens or dropped; the model reads interleaved items and actions. Retrieval predicts the next item; ranking predicts the action given the history and a candidate placed in the sequence. Called generative recommenders (GRs).
    • Layer. Each HSTU layer computes U,V,Q,K=Split⁡(ϕ1(f1(X)))U,V,Q,K=\operatorname{Split}(\phi_1(f_1(X)))U,V,Q,K=Split(ϕ1​(f1​(X))), then A=ϕ2(QK⊤+rabp,t)A=\phi_2(QK^{\top}+\text{rab}^{p,t})A=ϕ2​(QK⊤+rabp,t) and Y=f2(Norm⁡(AV)⊙U)Y=f_2(\operatorname{Norm}(AV)\odot U)Y=f2​(Norm(AV)⊙U), with ϕ1,ϕ2\phi_1,\phi_2ϕ1​,ϕ2​ the SiLU function and rabp,t\text{rab}^{p,t}rabp,t a relative bias for position and time gap. The attention is pointwise, not softmax-normalized, so the amount of relevant history is not normalized away; the same choice DIN made in 2018 (Inference: the paper does not draw this link). The gating by UUU plays the role of the explicit feature crosses of chapter 5.
    • Efficiency. Stochastic sequence-length truncation during training and an inference algorithm (M-FALCON) that scores many candidates in one pass by caching the shared history computation. The paper reports HSTU 5.3 to 15.2 times faster than FlashAttention2-based Transformers on 8,192-event sequences.
    • Reported scale and result Paper: models of 1.5 trillion parameters; a 12.4% improvement in online A/B tests on the paper's chosen metric; and a power-law fit of quality against training compute across three orders of magnitude, up to roughly GPT-3 / LLaMA-2 scale of training compute.

    How strong is this evidence?

    The architecture and offline results are public, and open-source implementations exist. The online gain and the production scaling curve are Meta's internal measurements against Meta's previous production system. That is the best evidence available for the scaling claim, but it is a single company's A/B test. The most significant claim is the scaling curve itself: if it holds elsewhere, recommendation quality becomes, like language modelling, mainly a matter of compute budget, which favours the largest platforms.

    End-to-end generative pipelines: OneRec

    Kuaishou's OneRec replaced the retrieve-then-rank cascade with a single generative model in production, the first public report of this at large scale. The February 2025 paper (“OneRec: Unifying retrieve and rank with generative recommender and preference alignment”, titled “…iterative preference alignment” on its arXiv listing) used an encoder–decoder with semantic IDs, a mixture-of-experts decoder that generates a whole session's list of videos, and a preference-alignment stage in which a reward model scores generated lists and the generator is tuned toward preferred ones (borrowing direct preference optimization from LLM alignment). The June 2025 technical report states Paper:

    • deployed in Kuaishou's main scenarios, handling about 25% of total queries per second;
    • stay time up 0.54% in the Kuaishou app and 1.24% in Kuaishou Lite;
    • operating cost about 10.6% of the traditional cascade's, and model FLOPs utilization of 23.7% in training and 28.8% in inference, far above typical cascaded rankers, because one large dense model replaces many small, memory-bound ones.

    Why the cost claim matters more than the engagement claim. A cascade runs dozens of models, most of them bottlenecked on memory lookups rather than arithmetic, so accelerators sit mostly idle. A single generative model is compute-bound and can use the same hardware and serving stack as LLMs. If the reported utilization generalizes, the economic case for generative recommendation is cheaper serving of a better model, not only better quality Inference.

    Foundation models for ads and recommendations

    In 2024–2025 the largest platforms described a common pattern: one or a few very large models trained on all user activity, whose knowledge is transferred into many smaller, task-specific serving models. Public descriptions, with their evidence grade:

    SystemDateWhat is describedEvidence
    X (Twitter) recommendation codeMar 2023Open-sourced pipeline: about 1,500 candidates per request from in- and out-of-network sources; a heavy ranker of about 48 million parameters (MaskNet-based); heuristics and filtersPost plus public code, the most inspectable production system of the period
    Meta AndromedaDec 2024Ads retrieval engine with deep neural networks co-designed for NVIDIA Grace Hopper; claims a 10,000× increase in model capacity for retrieval, +6% recall and +8% ads quality on selected segmentsPost
    Netflix foundation modelMar 2025A single large model trained autoregressively on member interaction histories, whose embeddings and fine-tuned variants feed downstream recommenders, explicitly inspired by LLM practicePost
    Meta GEMJul 2025 (call), Nov 2025 (post)Generative Ads Model, described as Meta's largest foundation model for ads ranking, trained at LLM-like scale; transfers knowledge to the vertical models that serve ads. Meta said GEM improvements raised ad conversions by about 5% on Instagram and 3% on Facebook Feed and Reels in Q2 2025Call for the conversion numbers; Post for the architecture
    LinkedIn 360BrewJan 2025A 150-billion-parameter decoder-only model that ranks from a text description of the member's history and the task, aiming to replace many task-specific models; the arXiv version was later withdrawnPaper (withdrawn preprint)

    The shared logic is economic. Serving latency caps the size of any model that scores every candidate, but training compute is not capped that way. A foundation model can be trained far beyond servable size and then used to produce embeddings, labels or soft targets for the servable models (knowledge distillation). This is the same split as Amazon's item table in 2003 (chapter 3), at a much larger scale: heavy work offline, light work at request time Inference.

    Ads in AI answers: the slot disappears

    Generative AI answers remove the ranked list of slots that thirty years of ad mechanisms assumed, and pricing and measurement for them are still being worked out. Google began showing ads within AI Overviews on US mobile search in October 2024 (desktop followed in 2025). OpenAI announced in January 2026 that it would test ads in ChatGPT for logged-in adult users in the US on its Free and Go tiers, with paid tiers remaining ad-free Post.

    Three questions are open Inference:

    • Allocation. A position auction needs slots with click rates αj\alpha_jαj​ (chapter 3). An answer has at most one or two placements and an influence on the answer itself, so the mechanism must price “mention” and “placement next to the answer” rather than position. Proposals in the research literature include auctions over LLM-generated text that mix advertisers' preferred outputs; none is a public production standard.
    • Measurement. Click-through is a weak signal when the answer already satisfies the user; incrementality tests (chapter 7) become the only credible measure of value, and they are expensive.
    • Trust. The answer's credibility is the product. Any ad that changes the answer, rather than appearing beside it, risks the core asset, which constrains ad load in a way that a feed of videos does not.

    Pre-mortem: how could Era V disappoint?

    Assume that by 2028 generative recommenders have not displaced cascades outside a few companies; the likely causes are already visible.

    • The scaling curve does not transfer. It was measured on one company's data and metric; smaller platforms have less data per user, and compute-optimal scaling may require data they do not have.
    • Serving cost meets advertising margins. Generating lists with beam search over long histories per request is expensive; the OneRec cost claim depends on replacing an inefficient cascade, which not every company runs.
    • Control. Cascades expose levers (filters, boosts, diversity rules, ad load) that product, policy and legal teams rely on; an end-to-end generator makes these harder to enforce and audit.
    • Measurement lag. Gains reported as attributed or modelled conversions may not survive incrementality tests (exercise D8).

    Even so, the direction from 1992 to 2026 has been consistent: each era replaced hand-designed structure with learned structure once data and compute allowed. Generative recommenders are the most extreme version yet, removing even the hand-designed boundary between retrieval and ranking.

    Exercises with worked answers

    In this chapter

    • Gist set (six problems, 30 minutes): the conceptual core of each era, with light arithmetic.
    • Depth set (eight problems, 30 minutes): the derivations from chapters 4–7, with numbers you can check by hand.
    • Try each before opening the answer; every answer ends with a check.

    The gist. If you can price a quality-weighted auction, de-bias a click log, explain why an autobidder may bid above value and grade a claim by its evidence, you have the gist path. The depth set tests whether you can redo the key derivations: the implicit-ALS saving, the watch-time odds, the logQ correction, budget multipliers, bid shading, delayed feedback and ESMM.

    Gist set

    G1 · Price a quality-weighted auction (chapter 3)

    Problem. One slot. Ad A bids $3.00 per click with predicted CTR 0.02; ad B bids $1.50 with CTR 0.05; ad C bids $2.00 with CTR 0.01. Who wins under Google's 2002 rule, what is the price per click, and what is the expected revenue per impression?

    Answer. Scores b⋅cb\cdot cb⋅c: A =$0.060=\$0.060=$0.060, B =$0.075=\$0.075=$0.075, C =$0.020=\$0.020=$0.020. B wins. Price pB=bAcA/cB=0.060/0.05=$1.20p_B=b_Ac_A/c_B=0.060/0.05=\$1.20pB​=bA​cA​/cB​=0.060/0.05=$1.20 per click. Expected revenue per impression 0.05×$1.20=$0.0600.05\times\$1.20=\$0.0600.05×$1.20=$0.060.

    Check: expected revenue equals the runner-up's score, as in chapter 3. Under GoTo's pay-your-bid rule ranked by bid, A would win and pay $3.00 per click, for expected revenue 0.02×3=$0.0600.02\times3=\$0.0600.02×3=$0.060: the same here, but with 40% of B's clicks and an unstable bidding game.

    G2 · Why item–item at Amazon (chapter 3)

    Problem. Give two reasons Amazon chose item-to-item filtering over user–user filtering.

    Answer. (1) Serving cost: with a precomputed similar-items table, the online cost depends only on the number of items the current user has bought, not on the number of customers or items. (2) Stability: item–item similarities change slowly and can be recomputed in batch, whereas a user's neighbourhood changes with every purchase and is noisy for users with few purchases.

    Check: the offline table costs O(N2M)O(N^2M)O(N2M) in the worst case, close to O(NM)O(NM)O(NM) in practice. The expensive work is moved offline, not removed.

    G3 · What the Netflix Prize taught (chapter 4)

    Problem. Netflix paid $1M for a 10.06% RMSE improvement but did not deploy the winning ensemble. Why, and what is the general lesson?

    Answer. The last few points of RMSE came from blending hundreds of models, which was expensive to engineer and maintain, and the business had moved to streaming, where what people play (implicit feedback, ranking of a page) mattered more than predicting star ratings. Netflix adopted two components (matrix factorization and RBMs). Lesson: an offline metric on a fixed dataset is a proxy, and the gap between proxy and business objective grows as the product changes.

    Check: the same lesson reappears in chapter 5's reproducibility audits and chapter 7's moving objectives.

    G4 · De-bias a click log (chapter 7)

    Problem. Examination probabilities are θ1=1.0\theta_1=1.0θ1​=1.0 and θ2=0.6\theta_2=0.6θ2​=0.6. Item D was shown 1,000 times at position 1 and clicked 70 times; item C was shown 1,000 times at position 2 and clicked 45 times. Which item is more relevant?

    Answer. Naive CTR: D 0.070, C 0.045. IPS-corrected relevance: D =70/1.0/1,000=0.070=70/1.0/1{,}000=0.070=70/1.0/1,000=0.070; C =45/0.6/1,000=0.075=45/0.6/1{,}000=0.075=45/0.6/1,000=0.075. C is more relevant and should be tried at position 1.

    Check: if C were at position 1 its expected clicks would be 1,000×1.0×0.075=75>701{,}000\times1.0\times0.075=75>701,000×1.0×0.075=75>70.

    G5 · An autobidder bids above value (chapter 6)

    Problem. Target CPA $50, pCTR 0.02, pCVR 0.05 (per click). Compute the value per 1,000 impressions. The campaign's budget is not binding and its learned multiplier is κ=1.2\kappa=1.2κ=1.2. What does it bid in a second-price auction, and why can that be consistent with the advertiser's target?

    Answer. Value per impression 0.02×0.05×$50=$0.050.02\times0.05\times\$50=\$0.050.02×0.05×$50=$0.05, i.e. $50 per 1,000. Bid 1.2×$50=$601.2\times\$50=\$601.2×$50=$60 CPM. The target constrains the average cost per conversion. In a second-price auction many impressions clear well below the bid, and the slack they create pays for impressions won above value, so the campaign buys more conversions while still averaging $50 per conversion.

    Check: with μ=0\mu=0μ=0, κ=(1+λ)/λ=1.2\kappa=(1+\lambda)/\lambda=1.2κ=(1+λ)/λ=1.2 gives λ=5\lambda=5λ=5; any λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 gives κ>1\kappa>1κ>1.

    G6 · Grade the evidence (chapter 1)

    Problem. Grade each: (a) “HSTU is a sequential transducer with pointwise rather than softmax attention.” (b) “A new ads model drove a 5% increase in conversions on Instagram last quarter,” said on an earnings call. (c) “Platforms with closed ecosystems lost less signal from ATT.”

    Answer. (a) Paper: an architectural fact stated in the ICML 2024 paper. (b) Call: management's attribution of a business metric; baseline, duration and measurement method undisclosed. (c) Inference: plausible from the mechanism, not a measured result in a cited source.

    Check: only (a) could be verified by someone outside the company, by reading the paper and code.

    Depth set

    D1 · How much the implicit-ALS trick saves (chapter 4)

    Problem. N=106N=10^6N=106 items, k=64k=64k=64 factors, and a user with nu=50n_u=50nu​=50 interactions. Compare the cost of forming Y⊤CuYY^{\top}C^uYY⊤CuY naively with the trick (counting multiply-adds, plus k3k^3k3 for the solve in both cases).

    Answer. Naive: k2N=4,096×106≈4.1×109k^2N=4{,}096\times10^6\approx4.1\times10^9k2N=4,096×106≈4.1×109. Trick: k2nu+k3=4,096×50+262,144=204,800+262,144=466,944k^2n_u+k^3=4{,}096\times50+262{,}144=204{,}800+262{,}144=466{,}944k2nu​+k3=4,096×50+262,144=204,800+262,144=466,944, with Y⊤YY^{\top}YY⊤Y computed once per sweep for all users. Ratio about 8,800×8{,}800\times8,800×.

    Check: the shared Y⊤YY^{\top}YY⊤Y costs the same 4.1×1094.1\times10^94.1×109 once, amortized over millions of users.

    D2 · Watch-time odds (chapter 5)

    Problem. In a feature cell, 200 impressions, 10 clicks, total watch time 1,500 s. What odds does the weighted logistic regression learn, and how close is it to expected watch time per impression?

    Answer. Odds =1,500/(200−10)=7.89=1{,}500/(200-10)=7.89=1,500/(200−10)=7.89 s. E[T]=1,500/200=7.5\mathbb E[T]=1{,}500/200=7.5E[T]=1,500/200=7.5 s and P=0.05P=0.05P=0.05, so odds =7.5/0.95=7.89=7.5/0.95=7.89=7.5/0.95=7.89, about 5% above E[T]\mathbb E[T]E[T].

    Check: the approximation E[T](1+P)=7.875\mathbb E[T](1+P)=7.875E[T](1+P)=7.875 is about 0.25% below the exact 7.89.

    D3 · Why logQ correction works (chapter 5)

    Problem. Items A and B both have raw score s=1s=1s=1. A appears in batches with frequency pA=0.02p_A=0.02pA​=0.02, B with pB=0.0002p_B=0.0002pB​=0.0002. Compute each item's corrected contribution es−log⁡pe^{s-\log p}es−logp to the softmax denominator when it appears, and the expected contribution per batch slot.

    Answer. A: e1−ln⁡0.02=e1+3.912=e4.912=135.9e^{1-\ln0.02}=e^{1+3.912}=e^{4.912}=135.9e1−ln0.02=e1+3.912=e4.912=135.9. B: e1−ln⁡0.0002=e1+8.517=e9.517=13,590e^{1-\ln0.0002}=e^{1+8.517}=e^{9.517}=13{,}590e1−ln0.0002=e1+8.517=e9.517=13,590. Expected contribution per slot: pA×135.9=2.718p_A\times135.9=2.718pA​×135.9=2.718 and pB×13,590=2.718p_B\times13{,}590=2.718pB​×13,590=2.718, both e1e^{1}e1.

    Check: in general ∑jpj esj−log⁡pj=∑jesj\sum_jp_j\,e^{s_j-\log p_j}=\sum_je^{s_j}∑j​pj​esj​−logpj​=∑j​esj​, the full-corpus normalizer. Without the correction, A would contribute 100 times more often than B as a negative, and the model would learn to push popular items down.

    D4 · Find the budget multiplier (chapter 6)

    Problem. Four impressions with (value, second-price cost) in dollars: (10, 4), (8, 6), (6, 2), (5, 4). Budget $8. Which impressions does the bid v/(1+μ)v/(1+\mu)v/(1+μ) buy, for what range of μ\muμ, and is that optimal?

    Answer. Win iff v/p≥1+μv/p\ge1+\muv/p≥1+μ. Ratios: 2.5, 1.33, 3.0, 1.25. Without a budget (μ=0\mu=0μ=0) all four are bought for $16 > $8. For 1.33<1+μ≤2.51.33<1+\mu\le2.51.33<1+μ≤2.5 the policy buys impressions 1 and 3, spends $6, surplus (10−4)+(6−2)=$10(10-4)+(6-2)=\$10(10−4)+(6−2)=$10. Enumerating feasible sets with spend ≤ $8: {1,3} $10; {1,4} $7; {2,3} $6; {3,4} $5; so it is optimal.

    Check: $2 of budget is unspent because impressions are indivisible; with many small impressions the threshold policy spends almost exactly BBB.

    D5 · Shade a first-price bid (chapter 6)

    Problem. Value v=$5v=\$5v=$5 CPM. (a) Highest competing bid Z∼Uniform(0,$8)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,\$8)Z∼Uniform(0,$8): optimal bid, win probability and expected surplus per 1,000 auctions, and compare with second price. (b) If ZZZ is the maximum of two independent Uniform(0, $8) bids, F(b)=(b/8)2F(b)=(b/8)^2F(b)=(b/8)2: optimal bid?

    Answer. (a) b∗=v/2=$2.50b^*=v/2=\$2.50b∗=v/2=$2.50; F=2.5/8=0.3125F=2.5/8=0.3125F=2.5/8=0.3125; surplus (5−2.5)×0.3125=$0.78(5-2.5)\times0.3125=\$0.78(5−2.5)×0.3125=$0.78. Second price, bid $5: v2/(2L)=25/16=$1.56v^2/(2L)=25/16=\$1.56v2/(2L)=25/16=$1.56. (b) F/f=(b2/64)/(2b/64)=b/2F/f=(b^2/64)/(2b/64)=b/2F/f=(b2/64)/(2b/64)=b/2, so 5−b=b/25-b=b/25−b=b/2, b∗=2v/3=$3.33b^*=2v/3=\$3.33b∗=2v/3=$3.33.

    Check: more competition shades less (2/3 of value instead of 1/2). With nnn uniform competitors, b∗=nv/(n+1)b^*=nv/(n+1)b∗=nv/(n+1), approaching truthful bidding.

    D6 · A click that has not converted yet (chapter 7)

    Problem. Eventual conversion probability p=0.04p=0.04p=0.04; delay exponential with rate λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5 per day (mean 2 days). A click has waited e=1e=1e=1 day without converting. What is the likelihood of that observation, and the probability it will still convert?

    Answer. e−0.5=0.6065e^{-0.5}=0.6065e−0.5=0.6065. Likelihood 1−p+pe−λe=0.96+0.04×0.6065=0.98431-p+pe^{-\lambda e}=0.96+0.04\times0.6065=0.98431−p+pe−λe=0.96+0.04×0.6065=0.9843. Probability of eventual conversion given none yet: pe−λe/0.9843=0.02426/0.9843=0.0246pe^{-\lambda e}/0.9843=0.02426/0.9843=0.0246pe−λe/0.9843=0.02426/0.9843=0.0246.

    Check: the click still carries 62% of its prior conversion probability (0.0246/0.04). Labelling it negative would throw that away.

    D7 · ESMM by hand (chapter 5)

    Problem. For an impression, pCTR = 0.02 and pCTCVR = 0.001. What is pCVR? Why is a CVR model trained only on clicked impressions biased when used to score all impressions?

    Answer. pCVR=0.001/0.02=0.05\text{pCVR}=0.001/0.02=0.05pCVR=0.001/0.02=0.05. Clicked impressions are a selected sample: users who click differ systematically from those who do not, so a model fitted on them learns P(conv∣click,x)P(\text{conv}\mid\text{click},x)P(conv∣click,x) only where clicks are common and extrapolates elsewhere. ESMM trains pCTR and pCTCVR on all impressions, and pCVR only through their ratio.

    Check: 0.02×0.05=0.0010.02\times0.05=0.0010.02×0.05=0.001; with 1,000,000 impressions that is 20,000 clicks and 1,000 conversions.

    D8 · Pre-mortem a generative-ads claim (chapters 7–8)

    Problem. A platform reports that a new foundation ranking model raised ad conversions by 5%. Twelve months later, advertisers' own holdout tests show no change in incremental sales. Give three mechanisms that would reconcile both facts.

    Answer. (1) Attribution, not incrementality: the model got better at reaching people who would have converted anyway, raising attributed conversions without causing more. (2) Measurement by the optimizer: reported conversions include modelled conversions from the same platform, so the metric partly moves with the model. (3) Mix and novelty: the A/B test ran on a favourable slice or a short window; gains decayed as advertisers' bids, budgets and competitors adapted (the auction is an equilibrium, not a fixed environment).

    Check: each mechanism predicts something testable: (1) attributed and incremental conversions diverge in a ghost-ad holdout; (2) observed-only conversions rise less than reported ones; (3) the lift shrinks with test duration.

    Glossary

    TermMeaning
    ALSAlternating least squares: fix one factor matrix, solve the other in closed form, repeat.
    ANNApproximate nearest-neighbour search (HNSW, product quantization, ScaNN).
    ATTApp Tracking Transparency: Apple's opt-in requirement for cross-app tracking, enforced from iOS 14.5 (April 2021).
    AutobiddingThe platform sets per-impression bids to meet an advertiser's budget and target CPA or ROAS.
    BPRBayesian personalized ranking: pairwise loss ln⁡σ(x^ui−x^uj)\ln\sigma(\hat x_{ui}-\hat x_{uj})lnσ(x^ui​−x^uj​).
    CalibrationPredicted probabilities match observed frequencies; required when predictions multiply bids.
    CPM / CPC / CPAPrice per 1,000 impressions / per click / per conversion (action).
    CTR / CVRClicks per impression / conversions per click.
    eCPMExpected revenue per 1,000 impressions; the common ranking currency across pricing types.
    FM / FFMFactorization machine / field-aware factorization machine.
    FTRL-ProximalFollow-the-regularized-leader online learner with per-coordinate rates and L1 sparsity.
    GSP / VCGGeneralized second-price auction / Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism.
    HSTUHierarchical sequential transduction unit: Meta's generative-recommender architecture (2024).
    IncrementalityConversions caused by the ad, measured by randomized holdout; contrast with attributed conversions.
    IPSInverse propensity scoring: reweight logged outcomes by the inverse probability of the logged action or exposure.
    logQ correctionSubtract the log sampling probability from logits when training with sampled (in-batch) negatives.
    oCPM / oCPCOptimized CPM / CPC: the advertiser targets outcomes, the platform sets impression or click bids with its predictions.
    ROASReturn on ad spend: attributed revenue divided by ad spend.
    RTBReal-time bidding: per-impression auctions on exchanges, standardized by OpenRTB.
    Semantic IDA short tuple of discrete codes for an item, built by quantizing its content embedding, so similar items share prefixes.
    SKAdNetworkApple's aggregated, delayed install-attribution API (from iOS 11.3, 2018).
    Two-tower modelSeparate user and item networks scored by a dot product, so item vectors can be indexed for ANN retrieval.

    Review record

    How the content was checked. Each chapter was drafted from the primary literature, then 50 specific dated or numeric claims were sent to two independent fact-checking passes that searched primary sources (papers, company posts, SEC filings, standards documents) without seeing the draft text. A third independent pass re-derived every formula, recomputed every worked example, exercise and chart, and checked 17 further claims; it found no substantive math errors, three wording slips in worked examples (fixed) and the content issues below.

    Claim in the first draftFindingChange made
    YouTube switched recommendations to watch time in October 2012Recommendations changed in March 2012; October 2012 was the search changeChapters 2, 5 and 7 now give March 2012 for recommendations and October for search
    OpenRTB 1.0 released in 2010 as the bidding protocolThe project started in late 2010; 1.0 was a narrower spec; the IAB adopted 2.0 in January 2012Chapters 2 and 6 cite the project start and the 2.0 adoption
